parts of the inserted sequence "align" with the reference sequence, giving an alternative description like `c.[850_869del;874_881del;887_897del;901_902insG]`

rulings.rationale:
This is decided for delins.md:47: write as one spanning delins, not individually — only for a minimal single delins that would otherwise be split because payload bases coincide with reference bases in the replaced span (the alignment-driven split delins.md:46 constructs and :47 rejects), and only in the NET-DELETION direction (payload shorter than the span). This is not a general license to merge separations of two or more; general.md:33 still governs elsewhere, and a row that does not fit this payload-coincidence net-deletion shape remains a violation. On the frameless DNA axes (g./m./n.), where general.md:34's codon exception can't apply, a row that does fit the shape is a disclosed rule-2 deviation, not a violation, per delins-payload-coincidence-carve-out-is-coding-dna-scoped.

This is governed by delins.md:47, which recommends the delins form for this shape (simpler, avoids incorrect protein-level predictions by tools), overriding general.md:33's "described individually" default. Neither clause is RFC-2119 normative, so this is a house choice within a gap the spec itself calls undesired, not a compliance finding.

The reason is that the spec constructs the split itself (:46) and then rejects it (:47), and that split's own separations are all two or more, so :17 read literally would force precisely the description :47 advises against, in the spec's own worked example -- proof by contradiction that :17 doesn't reach this shape. Candidate splits of this kind are also frequently non-unique, so adopting one trades a canonical form for an arbitrary pick from a family.

The net-insertion exclusion is kept, as a separate point: this ruling does not reach a block where the payload is LONGER than the span it replaces -- there the split form remains canonical. That is a mechanism fact, not a policy overlay: the :46 construction requires the payload's bases to be a subsequence of the span, which is impossible once the payload is longer, so the exclusion is largely redundant with the merge code's own embedding check rather than an independent choice riding on top of it. A rejected spec proposal whose own worked example was a net-insertion merge (SVD-WG010) is a negative guard against extending this ruling to that direction, not evidence for it.

The scope also covers any row where the interior of an otherwise-mergeable delins survives a candidate split only because payload bases coincide with reference bases -- not solely the literal :44-47 example -- provided the net-deletion direction and payload/reference-coincidence shape both hold.

Delegated, not decided here: which AXES the resulting merge reaches (c./g./m./n. vs r.) is answered by delins-payload-coincidence-carve-out-is-coding-dna-scoped, not by this record -- this record fixes shape and direction only.

One caveat: any prior figure for the cost of widening the net-insertion exclusion is unverifiable against current code; re-derive against the current mismatch budget and embedding gate before citing a number, never quote an old one. Pinned by `tests/it/spec_worked_example_rules.rs::the_spanning_delins_and_its_published_split_are_two_fixed_points`.

rulings.question: When a whole-span reverse complement competes with a multi-member description that is neither uniformly `delins` nor uniformly substitutions, but a mix of substitutions and multi-column members, which form is canonical?

clauses.quote: a sequence change where, compared to a reference sequence, **more than one nucleotide** replacing the original sequence is the reverse complement of the original sequence
the preferred description is: (1) substitution, (2) deletion, (3) inversion, (4) duplication, (5) insertion
descriptions removing part of a reference sequence and replacing it with part of the same sequence are not allowed
Allele: a series of variants on one chromosome.

rulings.rationale:
This is decided for the inv — a whole-span reverse complement is written as one inv even when the competing description mixes lone substitutions with multi-column members. This is a RULE 6 choice among conformant forms, not a conformance finding: inversion.md:5 defines an inversion as a property of the whole span (more than one nucleotide replaced by its reverse complement), so the inv is conformant; nothing compels it over the mixed competitor, which is conformant too. Rule 7's disclosure obligation is discharged by the introducing PR's Representation-Change trailer. Do not cite this as conformance, and do not read a build that emits the multi-member form as violating rule 1.

The ground is that notation must not turn on base coincidence. Refusing the inv on a tract whose competing split happens to contain a self-complementary interior column makes the description depend on a property of the SEQUENCE (whether that column happens to equal its own reverse complement) rather than of the EVENT — the same inversion over a tract with one fewer coincidental column would be spelled inv, this one would not. That instability is exactly what rule 6 is exercised to remove.

This does not run afoul of general.md:55 or :57. :55 ranks candidate type labels for ONE span; it does not rank members of a multi-member allele at all (decided separately, negatively, by conflicting-member-geometry-refusal-scope), and even read as reaching this case, every competitor here contains a substitution, which :55 ranks ABOVE inversion — so :55, if it reached this, would argue against the ruling, not for it. :57 prohibits removing part of a reference sequence and replacing it with part of the same sequence (i.e. a del beside a dup); it requires a del/dup/ins member, and the competing population here contains none, so it is not engaged either.

This record's outcome now stands as a special case of whole-span-reverse-complement-types-as-inv's uniform rule, which adopts the base-coincidence ground above. The prior claim that an all-substitutions competitor stays split under every gate is superseded by that record, and the piece-level gate this record widened is retired as dead code, not as wrong.

This does not settle: (1) whether general.md:55 reaches a multi-member allele at all — decided negatively elsewhere. (2) The frameless separation-one family (canonical arms merging across one unchanged nucleotide on axes with no reading frame): that shape is the rejected SVD-WG010 proposal and is a rule-1 conformance question, not a rule-6 choice. (3) The coding-axis merge questions, which are separate: the codon-frame merge at separation one (a defect), and the payload-coincidence carve-out at separation two-or-more (governed by delins-merge-vs-individual-gap-two-or-more). (4) inversion-vs-two-delins-76-83's all-delins competitor case, which reaches inv through the narrower gate and is untouched by this ruling.
rulings.summary: When a span replaced by its reverse complement competes with a description mixing lone substitutions and multi-column members, ferro writes it as one inv; both forms are conformant, so this is the project's choice among them.

rulings.question: Where the spec does not settle a normalization question, what ranks next — the reference implementation, the downstream consumer's already-shipped representation, or the filer's open issues?

clauses.quote: when a description is possible according to several types, the preferred description is: (1) substitution, (2) deletion, (3) inversion, (4) duplication, (5) insertion
HGVS recommendations try to avoid such conflicts wherever possible.
HGVS, therefore, recommends to describe translocations exclusively using a "delins" format.
The *major* version (`x`) will be incremented when changes are incompatible with existing conventions
The recommendations for the description of sequence variants are designed to be **stable**, **meaningful**, **memorable**, and **unequivocal**.
This is undesired; HGVS recommendations should be extended by specifying when to use which format.

rulings.rationale:
The canonical normalization ruleset is stated once, in docs/src/reference/normalization-rules.md (the documentation site) — this record does not restate it, and neither should CLAUDE.md or a PR body. One rule written in several places and drifting apart is this project's recurring failure mode; a fourth statement of it would be the bug, not a fix. This record instead holds the escalation register for the narrow case under the ruleset's rule 2: the spec expresses a preference among conformant forms, but supplies nothing to choose between the candidates that satisfy it. That is distinct from rule 5's much more common "spec is silent" case, which this register does not cover.

complex.md:63 ("HGVS recommendations try to avoid such conflicts wherever possible") states the value behind rules 5/6 — pick one form, retire the other — with :64 showing the method as a deliberate representation change.

An escalation must be (a) surfaced to the operator, never decided unilaterally by an agent or contributor; (b) documented here, naming the exact clause whose preference is being overridden and why no rule follows from it; and (c) locked by a unit test carrying an adjudication comment citing that clause. It is census-pinned (PRECEDENCE_ESCALATIONS in tests/it/hgvs_spec_normalization_tests.rs), so a new entry fails the build until the count is updated deliberately.

E1 is that delins is unranked: general.md:55 ranks substitution, deletion, inversion, duplication, insertion, and delins never appears; general.md:33 gives a separation test but no preference between two all-delins forms that both satisfy it. In scope, this is only the residue left after canonical-form-choice-when-both-legal (derive from the resulting sequence, then apply every explicit tie-break) — the case where derivation itself yields two all-delins candidates and the spec ranks neither. It is a typing question over already-derived candidates, never a license to keep the input's own partition. It is escalated, not decided.

Mutalyzer is not an authority here: its normalize endpoint re-derives from the mutated sequence and minimizes a weighted description length, not a spec rule — not guaranteed spec-compliant by its own maintainer's account — and where the spec is explicit, Mutalyzer is measurably wrong (it splits a case delins.md itself calls "not correct"). Live probes against real reference bases found no general separation disagreement — ferro and Mutalyzer split identically at separation one and two — and the one observed disagreement traces to Mutalyzer's weight model on a delins-shaped member, not to delins.md:47 on a genomic axis. Where ferro's own behavior was internally inconsistent between two such rows, resolving it removes that inconsistency in the direction ferro's shipped behavior already took on the simpler case — not a new divergence from the reference implementation.

Nor are the filer's issues a "direction": the requested fixes span merges, splits and respellings and are reconciled only by a method — derive from the resulting sequence — never by a preference for more or fewer members. That method is honored by canonical-form-choice-when-both-legal; it must not be traded against stability as though it were a member-count preference.

Confluence outranks stability because complex.md:63/:64's own method is pick-one-and-retire; the committee rejected an alternative explicitly for adding too many description options; and versions/index.md:48 calls cross-version incompatibility "known and intended," with no grandfathering language anywhere in the corpus. Disclosure — the ruleset's own rule — is the only remedy the spec offers.

Stability is only a tiebreaker: the clause sometimes read as guaranteeing description-level stability (basics.md:38) is grammatically about the rule set's own versioning, not about individual descriptions, and the corpus's only description-level use of "stable" concerns choosing a genomic reference to avoid transcript-model churn, not a spelling guarantee. The filer has said explicitly that stability isn't expected, asking only that instability be disclosed as a breaking change.

None of this settles which form to converge on where several remain conformant and the spec ranks none of them — that is E1, recorded rather than decided. Nor does anything here answer separation-is-a-property-of-the-spelling-not-of-the-variant, which is undecided.
rulings.summary: The canonical normalization ruleset is stated once, in ferro's reference documentation, and this record deliberately does not restate it — it holds only the escalation register for the rare case where the spec prefers one conformant form but supplies nothing to choose between the candidates that satisfy it.

rulings.question: When two descriptions of one variant are both legal under the recommendations, which one does ferro ship?

clauses.quote: It means that protein variant descriptions should be derived from comparing the variant protein sequence with the reference protein sequence.
the preferred description is: (1) substitution, (2) deletion, (3) inversion, (4) duplication, (5) insertion
This format is preferred when either of the two variants is known as a frequently occurring variant ("polymorphism").
the general HGVS rule of maintaining the longest unchanged sequence applies (the 3' rule)
two variants separated by one or more nucleotides should be described individually and **not** as a "delins"
Although the proteins resulting from the changes `NM_080877.2:c.1733_1735delinsTTT` and `c.1732_1794del` are identical, their HGVS description is different.

rulings.rationale:
Where two or more descriptions of one variant are legal and no spec clause selects between them, ferro derives the description from the RESULTING SEQUENCE and emits the form that falls out, subject to every explicit spec tie-break — never preserving the input's spelling, and falling back to the previously-shipped string only where re-derivation and every explicit tie-break still leave an unresolved tie.

This is governed by general.md:156, in its strongest form for protein descriptions — derive by comparing the variant and reference sequences; "knowledge on the underlying change on the DNA level should not be used." general.md:13 states the same for RNA/protein, and DNA/deletion.md:163 requires a description be unequivocal and carry no other information. Re-derivation is also the method the filer requested — a family of fixes spanning merges, splits and respellings, reconcilable only by "apply the edit set to the reference, then re-derive from the resulting sequence," not by any member-count preference.

Counter-evidence exists and is knowingly overridden: the spec elsewhere conditions a preferred form on provenance or population data not recoverable from the two sequences alone (DNA/delins.md:83's provenance rationale for splitting by default; RNA/delins.md:41 and the repeat pages' preference for known polymorphisms). Ferro cannot implement those and does not try; this ruling adopts the re-derivation half of the spec's self-contradiction deliberately.

Minimality is ferro policy, not a stated spec principle: several clauses (e.g. DNA/complex.md:50's "general HGVS rule of maintaining the longest unchanged sequence") cite length or simplicity as a REASON for a preference, but no minimality principle is stated as a rule, and delins.md:44-47 itself recommends a non-minimal spanning form in the spec's own worked example. Minimality guides derivation; it never overrides an explicit tie-break.

There is a residue this ruling does not reach: general.md:55 ranks five types (substitution, deletion, inversion, duplication, insertion) and omits delins, so it is silent on all-delins contests, and the spec doesn't even apply :55 uniformly (inversion.md:19 prefers insertion over duplication for inverted copies, against the ranking). Such cases fall through to re-derivation and then to adjudication-precedence-order's escalation register.

Nor is this a pure minimal-edit-distance partitioner — measured to degrade agreement with the reference implementation and to sharply increase release-to-release drift, and candidate minimal splits are frequently non-unique. Re-derivation must therefore pair with a deterministic tie-break among equally-minimal partitions; where the choice is arbitrary, it breaks toward the already-shipped form (adjudication-precedence-order rank 5).

The sharpest counter-evidence is recorded here so it isn't later mistaken for a refutation: protein/delins.md:50 keeps two DNA descriptions distinct even though the spec states the resulting proteins are IDENTICAL — the one case where the spec keeps forms apart on identical resulting sequences, which resulting-sequence derivation structurally cannot reproduce. This does not overturn the ruling.
rulings.summary: When two descriptions of one variant are both legal and no clause chooses between them, ferro applies the edit set to the reference and re-derives the description from the resulting sequence — subject to every explicit spec tie-break, and breaking any remaining tie toward the already-shipped form — rather than preserving the input's spelling.

rulings.question: `delins.md:18`'s exception names no edit type, but ferro applies it only to a substitution / unchanged base / substitution shape. Does the exception reach other shapes?

clauses.quote: **exception**: two variants separated by one nucleotide, together affecting one amino acid, should be described as a "delins"
**exception**: two variants separated by one nucleotide, together affecting one amino acid, should be described as a "delins"
when a variant can be described as a duplication, it **must** be described as a duplication and not as, e.g., an insertion

rulings.rationale:
The `DNA/delins.md:18` / `general.md:34` exception — "two variants separated by one nucleotide, together affecting one amino acid" — applies wherever that precondition holds, regardless of edit type, widening the rule: ferro's prior restriction to a substitution/unchanged-base/substitution shape is dropped as unjustified.

The ground for this is rule 3 of the normalization ruleset ("every rule is evaluated over the resulting sequence, never over the input's spelling"): edit type is a property of the spelling; "together affecting one amino acid" is a property of the resulting sequence. Gating the exception on edit type makes it spelling-dependent and therefore non-confluent — the same variant spelled two ways can get the exception once and not the other time. Rule 1 (conformance) independently supports this: the clause names no edit type, and no authority was ever produced for restricting it to one.

The widening has limits. It cannot cover a frameshift pair — a frameshift does not affect a single amino acid, so the precondition itself fails there; this is the clause's own precondition declining, not a shape carve-out. And `duplication.md:18` still governs: the widened rule must never turn a describable duplication (e.g. `c.[4C>T;5dup]`) into a delins.

Only half of this ruling is implemented, and that is load-bearing to note. `apply_coding_codon_exception` — the pass this ruling's direction actually widens — still matches only the substitution/unchanged-base/substitution triplet; it has not been changed. What shipped instead narrows a different, sibling pass (`merge::coalesce_coding_frame_separation`, which owns the length-changing block): that pass previously used a `length_changing` proxy and now tests the merged span's codon membership directly, which narrows rather than widens (some previously-merged non-substitution pairs now split). The two changes move output in opposite directions and must not be conflated.

The implemented half does not add this: the codon-membership predicate is edit-type-blind by design — a pair whose net length change is not a multiple of three can still merge if its span lies inside one codon. Whether "together affecting one amino acid" should additionally exclude such a pair (treating it as a frameshift affecting every downstream residue) is left open; a frameshift test there would be the same spelling-proxy problem pointed the other way.

One caveat: no known corpus row shows the un-widened restriction producing a wrong output; that is evidence of inertness on the corpora examined, not evidence the restriction was correct, and does not bear on the ruling.
rulings.summary: Two changes one nucleotide apart that together alter a single amino acid are ruled one delins whatever the edit types — because "together affecting one amino acid" is a fact about the resulting sequence, not about how the input was spelled — though the coding-codon pass currently implements only the substitution/unchanged-base/substitution triplet.

rulings.question: Do two variants separated by exactly one nucleotide, together affecting one amino acid, merge into a delins?

clauses.quote: **exception**: two variants separated by one nucleotide, together affecting one amino acid, should be described as a "delins"
**exception**: two variants separated by one nucleotide, together affecting one amino acid, should be described as a "delins" (e.g., `r.142_144delinsugg` `p.(Arg48Trp)`).
**exception**: two variants separated by one nucleotide, together affecting one amino acid, should be described as a "delins" (e.g., `r.142_144delinsugg` (`p.Arg48Trp`)).
The new recommendation will be: **two variants separated by less than two nucleotides should be described as a "delins"**.
Status: rejected

rulings.rationale:
Two changes one nucleotide apart that together affect a single amino acid are written as one `delins` on the coding sequence. `delins.md:18` is an explicit exception to the individual-description instruction at `:17`, stated in the same place and with the same scope -- no conflict to weigh, no deviation to record. `:19` gives the reason: leaving the two substitutions separate would let tools predict two conflicting consequences at one position, the same confluence argument this project makes elsewhere.

In scope: coding sequence only, and only within one amino acid (codon-precise, not merely "close together") -- applied after partitioning, triplet by triplet.

One precision note: the precondition is DISTANCE-based, never edit-type-based: a merge is licensed only if the merged piece's reference span stays within one codon, regardless of whether the underlying edits are substitutions, insertions, or deletions. Treating "length-changing" as a proxy for this test is wrong -- the codon-boundary test on the merged piece's own span is what governs, and it independently declines any merge that crosses a codon boundary. The identical exception sentence appears on every DNA and RNA recommendation page (`general.md:34`, `delins.md:18/81`, and the equal-length- and length-changing-page equivalents); `protein/delins.md:21` is the one page with no such exception.

One caveat, on dead text not to cite: `general.md:35-38`'s forward reference to a purely positional replacement rule is proposal SVD-WG010, which was REJECTED in 2021 and never removed from the page. It is not a live or pending rule; the codon-conditioned exception at `:18`/`general.md:34` is undiminished law.
rulings.summary: Two changes one nucleotide apart that together affect a single amino acid are written as one delins on the coding sequence, the explicit exception the spec makes to describing them individually.

rulings.question: When a duplication is already spelled on the far (3') side of an exon/exon junction — `LRG_199t1:c.3922dup`, which denotes the same transcript sequence as `c.3921dup` because both positions carry a `T` — must normalization shift it 5' back to `c.3921dup`, or is `c.3922dup` a legitimate description of a different genomic event that happens to yield the same transcript?

clauses.quote: the variant is described as `LRG_199t1:c.3921dup` (`NC_000023.10:g.32459297dup`) and not as `c.3922dup`
the variant (`NC_000023.11:g.32441180dup`) is **not described** as `c.3922dup` since this would shift the position of the variant to the next exon
an exception was made to prevent that when `c.3922dup` is translated back to a genomic position, one would end up at the wrong nucleotide, in the wrong exon
**exception**: deletions/duplications around exon/exon junctions using **c.**, **r.** or **n.** reference sequences

rulings.rationale:
A duplication is placed at the most 3' position that does not cross an exon/exon junction, reached from either side: a copy spelled past the junction is pulled back to it. `LRG_199t1:c.3922dup` normalizes to `LRG_199t1:c.3921dup`.

The grounds: `duplication.md:26`, `:60`, and `:148` state this outcome three times, independently, in three registers — the description rule itself, a note on a worked exon/exon example, and a Q&A giving the reason: translating the far-side spelling back to genomic coordinates lands "at the wrong nucleotide, in the wrong exon." That is a correctness reason, not a style preference.

The crux: `general.md:43` is not a blanket suspension of the 3' rule near a junction — it is directional, stopping the 3' rule from carrying a description across the junction. Leaving `c.3921dup` alone is `:43` working; also leaving `c.3922dup` alone is `:43` applied in one direction only. The clamp must bind from both sides: a description approaching the junction stops at it, and one already spelled past it is pulled back.

The scope covers deletions and duplications, on the `c.` and `n.` axes (and `r.` once upstream projection support lands). It does not reach `g.`, which has no junctions, and licenses no other 5' shift — the clamp is a boundary, not a general preference for 5' spellings.

The cost: this moves every stored far-side duplication spelling, including its projected genomic form; disclose as a breaking representation change (ruleset rule 7), not avoid it.
rulings.summary: A duplication is placed at the most 3' position that does not cross an exon/exon junction, reached from either side, so a copy spelled past the junction is pulled back to it.

guard.none: Undecided: the record puts upstream's own conflict on the record (`RNA/repeated.md:22` calls the shape invalid, `:27` publishes it) and names no side, so there is no ruling for a test to enforce. The record states in terms that ferro's present agreement with `:27` is an artifact of two independent passes rather than the question being decided, so pinning that agreement would read as enforcement of a ruling nobody made.

rulings.question: On an RNA reference, may a repeat be written with BOTH a position range and the repeat unit (`r.-6_-3g[6]`)? `RNA/repeated.md:22` marks that shape invalid as redundant; `:27` publishes exactly that shape as valid.

clauses.quote: the format r.-125_-123cug[4] should not be used; it contains redundant information (`-125_-123` and `cug`).
As such, `NM_024312.4:r.-6_-3g[6]` is valid as the reading frame is not affected.

rulings.rationale:
This is undecided: two clauses five lines apart conflict and cannot both hold. `RNA/repeated.md:22` states that a description carrying both a range and a unit is invalid, since the range already fixes the unit (example `r.-125_-123cug[4]`). `:27` then publishes `NM_024312.4:r.-6_-3g[6]` -- the same shape, range plus unit -- as the worked example of the UTR carve-out to the multiple-of-3 restriction. Whatever `:27` demonstrates, it demonstrates using a spelling `:22` forbids.

Ferro answers both ways by mode, and this is not the same as this record being decided: the plain library path (`parse_hgvs`, no preprocessing) leaves the published form alone, unchanged. `--error-mode strict` refuses the input. `--error-mode lenient`/`silent` currently emit `r.-6_-3g[6]` (the `:27` spelling) -- but only because a repair that keeps the unit and anchors the range gets handed to the normalizer, whose tract-maximization widens the anchor back onto the maximal repeat run in the reference, coincidentally reproducing `:27`'s string. That agreement is an artifact of tract maximization, not a conformance verdict; a prior repair (deleting the unit) landed on the `:22` answer, but only incidentally, for reasons unrelated to which clause governs.

What is not established: following `:22` over `:27` is the defensible reading -- a rule generalizes and a worked example does not, and `:22` states its reason -- but no path implements that reading deliberately, and the conflict is upstream's to resolve, not ferro's: either clause could be the one that is wrong. All three observed behaviors are pinned as observations, not reconciled as a ruling.

What would settle it is an upstream correction -- either `:22` carves out the UTR case, or `:27` is respelled as `r.-6_-3[6]`. Owed as a #466 entry against the HGVS nomenclature repository.

The scope: this record is about spelling redundancy only. The multiple-of-3 restriction `:24-27` is actually about is not in doubt -- ferro implements it exactly, including the UTR carve-out, and all of the spec's worked examples for it reproduce.

rulings.question: When a normalized cis allele leaves two members with no unchanged nucleotide between them, and both members consume reference bases, is that a description the recommendations admit?

clauses.quote: changes involving two or more consecutive nucleotides are described as deletion/insertion (delins) variants
changes involving two or more consecutive nucleotides are described as deletion-insertion (delins) so the description c.[79G>T;80C>T] is not correct
two variants separated by one or more nucleotides should be described individually and **not** as a "delins"
the preferred description is: (1) substitution, (2) deletion, (3) inversion, (4) duplication, (5) insertion
when a variant can be described as a duplication, it **must** be described as a duplication and not as, e.g., an insertion
Can I describe this variant as NM_007294.3:c.[2077G>A;2077_2078insTA]?
The correct description of this variant is `NM_007294.3:c.2077delinsATA`.

the answer was modified, i.e. the addition "However, since the variant is likely a combination of two other variants, it is acceptable to describe it as NM_007294.3:c.[2077G>A;2077_2078insTA]." was removed.
The correct description of this variant is `NM_007294.3:c.2077delinsATA`.
The correct description of this variant is `NM_007294.3:r.2077delinsaua`.
by definition, duplication may only be used when the additional copy is **directly 3'-flanking** of the original copy (a "tandem duplication").
a duplication of the sequence from nucleotide position `c.675-542` to `c.1211-703`, followed by the insertion of the sequence

rulings.rationale:
Two adjacent members that each consume reference bases (sub/del/delins/inv) are written as one delins, not split. This is governed by `docs/recommendations/DNA/substitution.md:32`, which renders the split spelling for such a pair `class="invalid"` and calls it "not correct" — the spec's own adjudication of this shape, not merely a type definition (`DNA/delins.md:16` defines the type but does not decide split-vs-merge).

This deviates from `docs/recommendations/general.md:55` (type prioritization), which a reader could invoke to keep a lone substitution adjacent to a delins separate. It is overridden because `:55` ranks the type of one description of one change; `delins` is absent from its list, and `substitution.md:32` is itself the counterexample to using `:55` this way.

The spec also states the merged answer independently, three times, for a substitution-adjacent-to-insertion instance (`DNA/delins.md:86-89`, `DNA/substitution.md:93-96`, `RNA/delins.md:68-71`): the split spelling was formerly permitted in the text and the permission was explicitly withdrawn — stronger than mere silence.

The scope here is load-bearing. It reaches only pairs where both members consume reference bases (sub/del/delins/inv on each side). `ins` on one side, a reference-consuming member on the other, merges into one delins (closed) — no clause protects the `ins` the way `duplication.md:18` protects a `dup`. Two true `ins` members sharing one junction are not reached — their order is genuinely undetermined; `general.md:78` supplies the designated spelling `ins[A;B]` for that content instead. Two junction-writing span edits (e.g. two `dup`s at one junction) are not reached either — nothing orders them and no clause glosses that pair, so it stays a conflict. A member that is a repeat-expansion (`N[n]`) adjacent to a reference-consuming member is untouched, and remains open.

The `dup` half of this raises two separate questions. First, may a `dup` and an adjacent `ins`/reference-consuming member sharing one junction be described together, or is it an overlap conflict? Decided: they may. `duplication.md:90` publishes exactly this shape — a `dup` abutting an insertion at its own junction — as a correct description, and `:91` glosses the order, which is the order whose absence the prior refusal was predicated on. Ferro accordingly accepts the pair rather than refusing it as an overlap conflict. Second, which form the accepted pair renders as — in particular, whether the output keeps the `dup` label rather than composing both payloads into one edit — is not decided here. `duplication-must-ranks-the-label-not-the-partition` establishes that no clause requires an edit set to be partitioned so as to produce a duplication, so keeping the split is legal and idiomatic but not mandated. This is additionally blocked on architecture, not adjudication: no existing pass holds both the reference window and the ability to split one edit into two at once, so choosing a form needs a new stage.

Two junction `dup`/repeat occupants stay registered for the interior-conflict test regardless of the above — an interior `ins` that the per-member pipeline respells as a `dup` must remain visible to that detector, or normalization becomes spelling-sensitive.
rulings.summary: Two adjacent changes that both consume reference bases are written as a single delins; the spec marks the split spelling "not correct" at separation zero.

rulings.question: The separation rule keys on the number of unchanged nucleotides between two variants, but two spellings of one variant can present different separations. On which of them is the rule to be evaluated?

clauses.quote: two variants separated by one or more nucleotides should be described individually and **not** as a "delins"
for all descriptions, the most 3' position possible of the reference sequence is arbitrarily assigned to have been changed
two variants separated by one or more nucleotides should be described individually and **not** as a "delins"
**The "delins" format is recommended**
the two variants may have been reported (or might occur) individually
one variant can be described using different formats. This is undesired; HGVS recommendations should be extended by specifying when to use which format.

rulings.rationale:
The separation `general.md:33` counts is read off the partition RE-DERIVED FROM THE RESULTING SEQUENCE, never off the input's spelling. Two spellings of one variant that differ only in how the edit set was split by the submitter converge on one output.

`general.md:33` and `delins.md:17` are stated over "two variants," which presupposes a decomposition — but a normalizer sees only the reference and the denoted sequence, not the submitter's split. Reading separation off the resulting sequence's own re-derived partition (rule 3 of the normalization ruleset, `docs/src/reference/normalization-rules.md`) is what makes the clause evaluable at all.

On `NC_000001.11:g.1001002-1001016` (`ATGAGGGGCCACTGT`), `g.[1001009del;1001010del;1001013del]` and `g.[1001009del;1001011del;1001013del]` both denote `ATGAGGGCATGT`. The ruling is `g.[1001009_1001010del;1001013del]`: over the individually-described competitor (reachable only by keeping the input's own member boundaries), by rule 3; over the single spanning `delinsCA`, by rule 2 (`general.md:33`/`delins.md:17`): the two members are separated by two unchanged bases and are both pure deletions with no gap-bearing member, so `delins-merge-vs-individual-gap-two-or-more`'s payload-coincidence carve-out does not reach this shape (`delins-recommendation-reach-when-the-input-arrives-split`) — on this axis or any other, the carve-out reaching every DNA axis notwithstanding.

This is a disclosed deviation from `delins.md:79-84`. The spec's stated reason for preferring individual descriptions there is provenance — "the two variants may have been reported (or might occur) individually" — which only the input's spelling carries. Ferro does not read provenance at runtime, so it cannot honor that reason; instead it picks one canonical partition per `(reference, sequence)` pair and evaluates `:33` on that partition. `open-issues.md:77-78` records the committee's own agreement that this is a real gap in the spec.

This does not settle which partition is canonical for a given `(reference, sequence)` pair: the method (re-derive from the resulting sequence, subject to explicit spec tie-breaks) is decided by `canonical-form-choice-when-both-legal`; the choice among equally-minimal partitions is left to `adjudication-precedence-order`. This record only makes `general.md:33` evaluable and confluent — it does not license reading separation off written positions anywhere else, and it does not adjudicate any contest whose competing forms are all reached by re-derivation. It does not decide the general canonical-partition question raised on the insertion side by `contiguous-insertion-split-by-a-blocked-derivation`.

One caveat: converging output on this basis moves stored representations wherever the partitioner previously preserved input-relative splits; disclose such moves as a breaking representation change (ruleset rule 7), not as a bug. Pinned by `tests/it/reported_confluence_pairs.rs::the_1420_v2_pair_does_not_converge_by_re_derivation`.
rulings.summary: Ferro reads the separation between changes off the partition it re-derives from the resulting sequence, not off the input's spelling, so two spellings of one variant converge on one output.

rulings.question: Does the negation in “should be described individually and not as a ‘delins’” carry prohibition force of its own, making `general.md:33` a ruleset rule 1 (Conformant, absolute), or does the modal grade the whole clause, making it rule 2 (Recommended form, best effort)?

guard.none: Decided and deliberately unguarded, because the ruling grades a clause rather than mandating an output: `general.md:33` is ruleset rule 2 in its entirety, and the record's own closing sentence is that this `changes classification only`. No description's normalized form turns on it, so there is no behaviour a test could fail on. What the grading buys is that a departure is a disclosable deviation rather than a rule-7 bug; that obligation is carried by the `Representation-Change` check and by the tripwires in `tests/it/codon_frame_deep_window_offset.rs`, whose module doc cites this record for exactly that reason — and neither of those fails if the grading itself is reversed.

clauses.quote: two variants separated by one or more nucleotides should be described individually and **not** as a "delins"
should preferably be described individually and not as a "delins" (unless they together affect one amino acid)
it **must** be described as a duplication and not as, e.g., an insertion
the description c.[79G>T;80C>T] is not correct
two variants separated by one or more nucleotides should be described individually and not as a "delins" of the sequence affected

rulings.rationale:
`general.md:33` is rule 2 (recommended form, best effort) in its entirety; its negation ("... and not as a 'delins'") does not carry prohibition force of its own. General reading: "and not Y" names the excluded alternative — it does not grade the clause. The modal grades the clause.

Three things support this. First, the two halves of the clause are complements — for variants separated by one or more nucleotides, "described individually" and "described as a delins" exhaust the available forms. If the delins form were forbidden, the individual form would be the sole permitted one, i.e. mandatory, and "should" would do no work. A clause cannot grade its positive half as a preference while forbidding the only alternative. Second, the spec restates this exact rule as a preference: `DNA/delins.md:81` (a Q&A block, adjudicative) answers "should **preferably** be described individually and not as a 'delins'" — same rule, same "and not", with "preferably" attached. Third, every rule-1 prohibition marker ("must", "not allowed", `class="invalid"`) is absent from all five places the spec states this rule.

Where the spec does prohibit is at separation ZERO: it marks the split spelling `class="invalid"` and calls it "not correct" (`DNA/substitution.md:32`) — the ground already used in `delins-adjacent-members-when-both-consume-reference`. So: separation zero is a prohibition; separation one or more is a preference. This record reads that line, it does not move it.

What this does not license: rule 2 still outranks maintainer judgment, so ferro remains obliged, on best effort, to produce the individual form. What changes is classification only: merging across one or more unchanged nucleotides on a frameless axis is a rule-2 miss to disclose and pin as a deviation, not a rule-1 bug — it does not by itself block a release. Every negative guard measuring such a deviation must stay pinned at its true value with a tripwire that fails if a listed row starts conforming (the `FERRO_IS_WRONG` shape); re-pinning a guard to zero to get a green build is the one move this record forbids.

In scope, these are rulings on the FORCE of the separation rule and on the reading of "and not" generally. It does not decide which form ships where several remain legal (`canonical-form-choice-when-both-legal`), the reach of the codon exception (`projection-codon-exception-is-decided-by-the-rendered-axis`), or `delins.md:47`'s carve-out (`delins-payload-coincidence-carve-out-is-coding-dna-scoped`). Nor does it disturb `delins-merge-vs-individual-gap-two-or-more`, which scopes when `:33` yields to `delins.md:44-47`; this record is about how strongly `:33` speaks when it does apply.
rulings.summary: Two changes a nucleotide or more apart are described individually — this is the spec's preference (ruleset rule 2), not an outright ban; the only spelling the recommendations forbid is the split at separation zero.

rulings.question: #1616 merges eight coding-axis multi-member alleles whose members are authored two or more unchanged nucleotides apart. `general.md:33` and `DNA/delins.md:17` say such members are described individually. Is that a deviation to disclose, or does `general.md:33` fail to reach a partition that re-derives to a single member?

clauses.quote: two variants separated by one or more nucleotides should be described individually and **not** as a "delins"
two variants separated by one or more nucleotides should be described individually and **not** as a "delins"
**The "delins" format is recommended**: it is simpler and prevents software tools making incorrect predictions for the consequences on protein level.
**exception**: two variants separated by one nucleotide, together affecting one amino acid, should be described as a "delins"
should preferably be described individually and not as a "delins" (unless they together affect one amino acid)

rulings.rationale:
An operator ruling: the eight coding-axis merges ferro introduced when it removed the input-relative weight bound ARE a `general.md:33` deviation — ferro emits one spanning `delins` where `:33` says to describe the members individually. It is recorded as a deviation, not a re-reading or a carve-out, and the remedy is disclosure plus a tripwire, not a block.

The rows are pure deletions deriving to one member, so nothing is inserted: `DNA/delins.md:47` (which reaches an inserted sequence) does not apply, `DNA/delins.md:17` and `general.md:33` govern unqualified and call for individual members, and `general.md:34`'s codon exception does not reach a separation of two or more. The merge happens anyway, and `derivation-may-not-be-bounded-by-the-inputs-spelling` states that removing the weight bound does not license the merges it had been blocking — so that change is no authority for them.

`separation-rule-force-modal-or-negation` grades `general.md:33` a whole-clause rule 2, whose remedy is disclosure plus a tripwire, not a release block. The schema roles are split because the build refuses one clause being both authority and departure: `DNA/delins.md:81`, which states the rule with "preferably", governs, while `general.md:33` and `DNA/delins.md:17` are what ferro deviates from — `:33` still reaches the rows.

The id is a name, not a citation: it says `general-34` while the clause is `general.md:33` (a spec-checkout bump shifted the line), and it is cited by exact string from other records and Rust prose, so it must not be renamed to chase a line number that will move again.

The tripwire is `coding_axis_separation_two_or_more_merges` in `tests/it/spec_conformance_axis.rs`, checked in both directions; any change to the pin must name the clause or ruling that carried it, since the count is a set to re-derive — a row that gains a gap-bearing member leaves it — not a constant to defend. Measured on the current partition rule that set is empty: the eight original rows have left it and the rows now counted are non-deviations, so the disclosure is vacuous and the record awaits an operator decision to narrow it to its original base or retire it. Changing its status is an operator act.
rulings.summary: A disclosure that currently fires on nothing: it records a rule-2 deviation from the spec's preference to describe members individually — a coding-axis merge of allele members two or more unchanged nucleotides apart with no gap-bearing member — but on the current partition rule that set is empty, so the record is a candidate for narrowing or retirement rather than a live rule.

rulings.question: A single contiguous insertion inside a tandem tract can be spelled as an insertion at one junction plus a duplication inserting at the next, with one unchanged reference base between them. Does `general.md:33` license that two-member description?

clauses.quote: two variants separated by one or more nucleotides should be described individually and **not** as a "delins"
**3'rule**: for all descriptions, the most 3' position possible of the reference sequence is arbitrarily assigned to have been changed.
the preferred description is: (1) substitution, (2) deletion, (3) inversion, (4) duplication, (5) insertion
when a variant can be described as a duplication, it **must** be described as a duplication and not as, e.g., an insertion
one variant can be described using different formats. This is undesired; HGVS recommendations should be extended by specifying when to use which format.

rulings.rationale:
A single contiguous insertion spelled as an insertion plus a duplication one base apart, at a locus with only one underlying variant, is written as the one insertion — not split into two members.

This is governed by `docs/recommendations/general.md:33`, stated over "two variants". This locus carries only one: aligning the sequences the two spellings denote leaves a single contiguous inserted run plus, where present, a separate distant edit; the apparent unchanged base between the "two" members is an artifact of an ambiguous tract letting the inserted bases be dealt out on either side of it. `:33` therefore does not reach this shape at all — there is no pair of variants for it to keep separate.

That the re-derived single-member form is what ships follows from `canonical-form-choice-when-both-legal` (derive from the resulting sequence, don't preserve the input's spelling) and is not re-decided here.

No tie-break rescues the split. `duplication.md:18` (must describe a describable duplication as one) does not apply — the inserted sequence is not actually a copy of either adjacent reference run, so it isn't describable as a duplication in the first place. `general.md:55` (type-priority ranking) ranks the type of one description of one variant; invoking it to justify the two-member split begs the question of accepting that decomposition.

This is a load-bearing status point: it is a DECIDED ruling that is NOT yet implemented. Ferro currently produces the multi-member form as a non-confluence side effect: the same underlying variant normalizes to two different stable strings depending on shuffle direction, whenever a third, distant member elsewhere in the allele blocks the sequence-first derivation from firing (without that third member, ferro already merges to the single insertion on its own).

The representation effect: implementing this moves any stored allele whose members are a junction-adjacent insertion+duplication pair beside a third member far enough away to currently block the derivation, from the multi-member spelling to the single insertion. No output changes yet.
rulings.summary: A single contiguous insertion spelled as an insertion plus a duplication one base apart is ruled to be the one insertion, because the separation rule keys on two variants and this locus carries only one — a decided target not yet implemented, so ferro still emits the multi-member form when a distant third member blocks the derivation.

rulings.question: Does `general.md:57`'s prohibition on removing part of a reference sequence and replacing it with part of the same sequence reach the `::`-joined segments of a ring chromosome, as it reaches the members of a `[a;b]` cis allele?

clauses.quote: when a description is possible according to several types
descriptions removing part of a reference sequence and replacing it with part of the same sequence are not allowed
"::" is used to indicate the join, instead of ";" to describe two not connected deletions
a range of changes occur that can not be described as one of the basic variant types
a double colon is used to designate break point junctions creating a ring chromosome.
Break point location is determined by the first break point encountered, i.e. `pter` of the chromosome is to be listed first.
multiple breakpoints in one chromosome are listed in order of occurrence from `pter` to `qter`.
variant descriptions are always in the forward orientation (from `pter` to `qter`, the end of the chromosome), determined by the chromosomal origin of the intact centromere (`cen`).

rulings.rationale:
general.md:57's prohibition — replacing part of a reference sequence with part of itself — does not reach the '::'-joined segments of a ring chromosome description; ferro keeps a ring's members rather than collapsing them to a linear delins.

:57 doesn't reach it because :57 is a sub-bullet of :55, the type-prioritization rule, and works by REDIRECTING to a preferred single-type description when one is possible (its own example: a del beside a dup redirects to a delins over the union span) — a redirection clause, not a hygiene clause, whose antecedent requires a competing single-type description to redirect toward. complex.md:5 defines complex changes as exactly those that CANNOT be described as one basic type, so no such competitor exists for a ring; a delins over the union span would describe a LINEAR product and silently discard the join, which is the entire content of the ring description.

The operators themselves are governed directly by complex.md:130 — '::' indicates the join, ';' describes two unconnected deletions, on identical member content. The same two deletions spelled with ';' denote a linear chromosome missing both ends; with '::' they denote a ring. The composite carries a topological assertion the members alone don't, so reading ring segments as ordinary cis-allele members is exactly what the spec forecloses.

In scope, this exempts no edit from :57 — it only declines to read '::' as ';': a same-chromosome ring has exactly two breakpoints and its segments are telomere-anchored and disjoint by construction, so the self-cancelling check would rarely even fire on a well-formed ring; and a rearrangement-plus-local-edit composite is spelled as a ';' cis allele, not as an extra '::' segment, where :57 still governs normally.

This does not settle, and must not be read as blessing, the fact that ferro currently accepts some non-well-formed '::' rings (no telomere anchor, wrong pter-to-qter segment ordering, or a dup contributing no break junction). Those are ring WELL-FORMEDNESS defects needing their own rule — :57 is the wrong instrument for them (it would wrongly accept a non-overlapping malformed case, and would emit a "rewrite as delins" repair hint that complex.md:5 makes actively wrong advice for a ring).
rulings.summary: The prohibition on replacing part of a sequence with part of itself does not reach the '::'-joined segments of a ring chromosome, so ferro keeps a ring's members rather than collapsing them to a linear delins.

rulings.question: `background/standards.md` lists `X` and `-` in the DNA symbol table and daggers both, footnoting them at `:39` as used in alignment only. May a description state one of them, and if not, is refusing it a conformance requirement or a style preference?

clauses.quote: masked nucleotide
gap of indeterminate length
used in alignment only
nucleotides in CAPITALS using [IUPAC-IUBMB assigned nucleotide symbols]

rulings.rationale:
`X` and `-` are refused in a description; `background/standards.md:39` governs. Neither is among the IUPAC-IUBMB nucleotide symbols a description may use.

This is not a conflict with `:36`/`:37`, which list `X` and `-` in the DNA symbol table: each is daggered (`X†`, `-†`), and `:39` is that dagger's own annotation — scoping both symbols to alignment — not a separate, competing clause. Reading `:36`/`:37` without the dagger is reading half the table row.

The wording's strength doesn't matter here either way: the alphabet half of rank-1 validity decides this independently of how strongly `:39`'s prohibition is graded. `general.md:47` requires assigned IUPAC-IUBMB symbols, and `X` is not one of the fifteen. So the shape fails the grammar under either reading of `:39`.

Measured: `c.10delinsX` denotes no sequence under an independent applier — there is nothing for a lenient mode to be lenient toward. Ferro currently accepts and re-emits it in both input-hygiene modes on every reference shape; `-` is already refused at parse, so this ruling asks for consistency with behavior ferro already has for `-`, not new machinery.

This settles WHAT (refuse), not WHERE — the enforcement stage is `absolute-prohibition-enforcement-stage` (decided): strict fails at parse, lenient fails only when it cannot normalize.

In representation terms there is no impact: no input that currently normalizes to a legal description changes; only currently-invalid outputs are affected. Pinned by `tests/it/corpus_prohibited_inputs.rs::an_alignment_only_symbol_is_refused_in_every_mode_for_both_x_and_dash`.
rulings.summary: The alignment-only symbols 'X' and '-' are refused in a description, since they are not among the IUPAC-IUBMB nucleotide symbols a description may use.

rulings.question: `checklist.md:20` says an `NM_` reference can describe an intronic position only when a genomic reference sequence is given. Must ferro refuse a bare `NM_…:c.20+2del`, and in which input-hygiene mode?

clauses.quote: can only be used to describe variants in introns using a `c.` prefix when a genomic reference sequence is given
this describes a deletion of nucleotide -14 in the intron directly 5' of nucleotide `c.12`
**exception**: deletions/duplications around exon/exon junctions using **c.**, **r.** or **n.** reference sequences

rulings.rationale:
A bare transcript intronic position (e.g. `NM_...:c.20+2del`) is refused in strict input-hygiene mode (`IntronicOnBareTranscript` / `W4007`) and accepted in lenient mode.

This is governed by `checklist.md:20`, a CONDITIONAL clause, not absolute. It is phrased "can only be used ... when" — a condition on the reference sequence (a genomic reference must be given), not a prohibition — and lacks the checklist's prohibitive vocabulary ("is not allowed", "Not correct") used four items on either side of it.

The ruling weighs counter-evidence: the spec itself glosses a bare-`c.` intronic description at `:45` (`c.12-14del`, explaining the string's meaning) with no genomic wrapper — a clause the spec does not apply to its own worked example cannot be read as an absolute bar on the spelling. `general.md:43`'s exemption for junction-adjacent variants on bare `c./r./n.` axes is a third side, cited as context rather than support: it shows the spec contemplates that axis near an intron rather than settling this clause's force.

This governs INPUT: a description the user already spells with a bare intronic transcript position. It does not license ferro's own normalizer emitting such a bare form as OUTPUT — where ferro's shuffle crosses an exon/intron junction and would otherwise manufacture a bare intronic transcript coordinate, that output is instead wrapped against the genomic reference the crossing resolved to. An input that already names a bare intronic position is still accepted verbatim in lenient mode and refused in strict, per the ruling above.

The representation impact is none — this ratifies shipped behavior in both modes. Pinned by `tests/it/corpus_prohibited_inputs.rs::a_bare_transcript_intronic_position_is_refused_in_strict_only`.
rulings.summary: A bare transcript intronic position such as 'NM_...:c.20+2del' is refused in strict input-hygiene mode and accepted in lenient mode, since the spec allows it only when a genomic reference is given.

rulings.question: `general.md:57` prohibits one member-vs-member geometry outright and illustrates it with a `del` beside an overlapping `dup`. Does the prohibition reach the CLASS of alleles whose members claim intersecting reference territory — nested, partially overlapping, and two insertions at one interbase — or only the edit-type pair it names?

clauses.quote: Allele: a series of variants on one chromosome.
descriptions removing part of a reference sequence and replacing it with part of the same sequence are not allowed
the preferred description is: (1) substitution, (2) deletion, (3) inversion, (4) duplication, (5) insertion
designed to be **stable**, **meaningful**, **memorable**, and **unequivocal**

rulings.rationale:
Two members of one allele that claim intersecting reference territory — nested, overlapping, or two insertions at one interbase — are refused, whatever edit types they render as. Rank-1 validity under `adjudication-precedence-order`; not tradeable against representation.

This is governed by `docs/recommendations/DNA/alleles.md:5` (an allele is "a series of variants on one chromosome"), not `:57`. `:57` is the spec's only explicit member-vs-member prohibition, but its stated ground ("removing part of a reference sequence and replacing it with part of the same sequence") literally describes only its own worked example, a deletion beside a duplication — read strictly it would not reach two nested deletions. The definitional clause reaches the whole class: two members writing to one reference interval describe no single chromosome sequence for an allele to be read off (`basics.md:38`'s "unequivocal").

`general.md:55` is cited here to record that it does NOT apply — it ranks the type of one description of one span, not two members of one allele. Citing `:55` against a multi-member allele is a recorded error to guard against (`:55`/`:57` are adjacent lines and easy to conflate).

The argument runs per geometry:
- Overlapping: `:57`'s own geometry — direct textual evidence.
- Coincident insertions at one interbase: un-denotable — two zero-width members with no order give different sequences depending on order; even with identical payloads the ambiguity persists as multiplicity (two insertions vs. one stated twice), so an "orders agree" test would wrongly admit the identical-payload case.
- Nested: the weakest geometry — the inner member of a nested pair could be argued redundant (entailed by the outer) and absorbed. Refuted: an otherwise-identical nested pair with a non-redundant inner payload (a `delins` instead of a `del`) has nothing redundant about it, so an absorbing rule would have to inspect payloads and give geometrically identical spellings opposite verdicts. The rule must be geometric, not payload-dependent.

As for status: ferro already refuses this class in strict mode (`OverlapConflictingEdits` / `W5002`); `:57`'s own spelling is refused earlier still, at parse, in both modes. Lenient mode preserving the conflict verbatim is a separate, deliberate contract and is not reopened here. The stage (strict-parse refusal, uniformly) is settled by `absolute-prohibition-enforcement-stage`.
rulings.summary: Two members of one allele that claim intersecting reference territory — nested, overlapping, or two insertions at one interbase — are refused, whatever edit types they render as.

rulings.question: The checklist enumerates the spec's absolute prohibitions. Is a violation to be refused at PARSE — unconditionally, in every mode — or at strict-mode normalize, where a caller can opt out of it?

clauses.quote: **do not correctly follow HGVS nomenclature**
can not have nucleotides with additions like a `+`, `-`, or `*`
is **ambiguous**, and not allowed
is not allowed, the inserted sequence

rulings.rationale:
Enforcement of an absolute prohibition is mode-dependent, uniformly across every prohibited spelling: strict refuses at parse; lenient does not check input conformance at parse, instead repairing the input where possible and refusing only if normalization itself cannot succeed; and silent behaves the same as lenient, but with no warning/error messages, only an exit code.

This is governed by `docs/recommendations/checklist.md:5`, which defines the checklist as a catalogue of descriptions that "do not correctly follow HGVS nomenclature" — a property of the input, and therefore input-hygiene's business rather than the grammar's. The spec does not address enforcement stages at all; this is a maintainer decision under rule 6 of the normalization ruleset, disclosed under rule 7.

Lenient mode does not trade away rule 1. Rule 1 ("output follows the HGVS recommendations; absolute — never traded") binds on output in every mode, with no flag that turns it off: the prohibited spelling may never be emitted. Accepting a non-conformant input and normalizing it to a conformant output trades nothing away — that is the ordinary business of a normalizer, which is what lenient mode is for. The mode gate governs whether the input is judged at parse; it never governs whether the output conforms.

There is a disclosed departure carved out here. `background/numbering.md:52-53` numbers the non-coding axis only `n.1...n.last` plus intronic offsets — it has no `*` (past-the-end) zone and no `-` (upstream) zone of its own, unlike `c.`. Both `n.-N` and `n.*N` are therefore out-of-zone, but they are not enforced the same way: `n.-N` follows the uniform mode gate above, refused at strict parse only, while `n.*N` is refused at parse unconditionally, in every mode, including lenient and silent. This is a deliberate, disclosed departure from the uniform rule, not an oversight: real-world `n.-N` usage exists (upstream-promoter and similar variants), so tolerance is worth keeping; no corresponding real-world `n.*N` usage has been found, so the unconditional refusal breaks nothing observed. It is revisitable — a reported real `n.*N` usage is grounds to move it onto the `n.-N` schedule. The tempting justification that `n.*N` is a pure grammar non-position rather than a conformance matter is explicitly not the ground for the carve-out, because it proves too much: it would equally exempt `g.*10` (`checklist.md:16`), which stays mode-gated like everything else.

What this does not settle: whether a given shape is invalid at all is settled elsewhere (see `alignment-only-symbol-in-a-description`, `conflicting-member-geometry-refusal-scope`). Which repair lenient mode should choose when more than one is legal is `canonical-form-choice-when-both-legal`.
rulings.summary: Spellings the spec prohibits are rejected — at parse in strict mode; lenient mode instead repairs the input where it can and fails only if it cannot normalize.

rulings.question: Must a ring chromosome's first `::` segment start at `pter` and its last end at `qter`, so that a ring whose segments name only interior coordinates is refused?

guard.none: Undecided: the record asks whether a ring naming only interior coordinates must be refused, and answers neither way. `tests/it/ring_segment_wellformedness.rs::a_ring_with_no_telomere_anchor_is_still_accepted` pins today's acceptance, which the record itself calls the status quo rather than a ruling — it would go on passing under one answer and would have to be deleted under the other, so it is not this record's guard.

clauses.quote: the start of the chromosome is described as `pter`, the end as `qter`, and the centromere as `cen`
the description of complex changes can become rather complicated and at some point, although literally correct, becomes effectively meaningless

rulings.rationale:
A ring chromosome forms from two breaks whose ends fuse, losing both telomeres; a well-formed ring is therefore anchored at `pter` and `qter`, and both ring examples the spec publishes are so anchored (`:127`, `:161`). But no clause states this as a requirement: `complex.md:28` defines what `pter`/`qter` mean without requiring them, and `:13` warns that a complex description can be "literally correct" yet meaningless -- cutting against inventing a structural requirement the text doesn't carry. Two worked examples are a thin basis for a rejection rule (a sibling rule in this project over-generalized from one clause this way and broke a published legal-edit control before independent support was found for it), so this stays open rather than being decided by analogy.

As current behavior, not a ruling: ferro accepts an unanchored ring -- `g.100_200del::300_400del`, `g.pter_14700000del::37600001_40000000del`, and `g.100_14700000del::37600001_qterdel` all parse and round-trip.

What would settle it is either a clause requiring the anchors, or a real description in which an unanchored `::` join is meaningful.

One caveat: `:28`'s `(pter)_#`/`#_(qter)` forms and `cen` mean any anchor test is not a simple "is the first endpoint `pter`" check; `cen`-anchored segments do not currently parse at all, so enforcing risks a false rejection beyond the anchor question itself.

rulings.question: `delins.md:47` recommends the single `delins` where a split exists only because payload bases coincide with reference bases. Which axes does that carve-out reach?

clauses.quote: two variants separated by one or more nucleotides should be described individually and **not** as a "delins"
two variants separated by one nucleotide, together affecting one amino acid, should be described as a "delins"
it is simpler and prevents software tools making incorrect predictions for the consequences on protein level
This restriction only applies to the coding sequence, which does not include the introns or the UTR sequence
two variants separated by one or more nucleotides should be described individually and **not** as a "delins"
the 3'rule applies to ALL descriptions (genome, gene, transcript, and protein) of a given variant
Status: rejected
making a discrimination between variants in protein-coding and non-coding sequences

rulings.rationale:
`delins.md:47`'s payload-coincidence carve-out — merging a split into one spanning delins where the split exists only because payload bases coincide with the reference — reaches every DNA axis: `c.`, `g.`, `m.`, `n.`. It does not reach `r.`.

It governs on the coding axis because `:47`'s stated reason is preventing incorrect protein-level predictions; the worked example is a coding row (`LRG_199t1:c.850_901`); the neighbouring exception at `:18` is codon-bound. That reasoning does not extend past the coding axis on its own.

It was widened to all DNA axes as a house choice: `:47` gives a second, axis-neutral ground — "it is simpler". Nothing in that ground refers to a reading frame or protein consequence. The widen rests on that ground alone, under `normalization-rules.md` rule 6, as a house choice among conformant forms the recommendations permit — not a conformance finding. No clause compels the single spanning form off the coding axis; do not cite this record as though one did.

Counter-evidence the ruling overrides: on the frameless axes (`g.`/`m.`/`n.`) there is no reading frame, so this carve-out's payload-coincidence shape is indistinguishable from the general "two variants separated by two or more nucleotides" shape the SVD-WG010 proposal asked to merge on the identical simplicity ground — and that proposal's `Status: rejected`. So on those axes this widen is, in substance, adopting a rejected proposal's outcome one shape at a time: it is a disclosed RULE-2 DEVIATION from `general.md:33`/`DNA/delins.md:17` (same classification as `coding-axis-merges-are-a-disclosed-general-34-deviation` and `separation-rule-force-modal-or-negation`), never a rule-1 correction.

`r.` is excluded on jurisdictional grounds: a `DNA/` document has no authority over the RNA axis regardless of how widely its DNA-side scope is drawn, and `RNA/delins.md` states no `:47` counterpart of its own — no merge rationale, no exception. There is no RNA clause to carry this carve-out.

One implementation caveat: the gate must key on axis KIND (DNA vs RNA), not on `AxisFrame::reading_frame` / the frame flag used elsewhere — that flag is true for a coding-RNA description too, and keying on it would silently extend this DNA-only carve-out onto `r.`, which this record does not reach.
rulings.summary: Where a split exists only because payload bases coincide with the reference, ferro writes it as one spanning delins on every DNA axis (c./g./m./n., but not r.); on the frameless axes this is a disclosed rule-2 deviation and the project's choice among conformant forms.

rulings.question: `DNA/delins.md:44-47` recommends the spanning `delins` where parts of the payload align with the reference, while `:17` and `general.md:33` describe separated variants individually. `canonical-form-choice-when-both-legal` settles that the input's spelling does not decide. Which of the two clauses then selects the form a re-derivation must land on?

clauses.quote: **The "delins" format is recommended**: it is simpler and prevents software tools making incorrect predictions for the consequences on protein level.
parts of the inserted sequence "align" with the reference sequence, giving an alternative description like `c.[850_869del;874_881del;887_897del;901_902insG]`
two variants separated by one or more nucleotides should be described individually and **not** as a "delins"
two variants separated by one or more nucleotides should be described individually and **not** as a "delins"
one variant can be described using different formats. This is undesired; HGVS recommendations should be extended by specifying when to use which format.

rulings.rationale:
A re-derived split merges into one `delins` under `delins.md:46-47` only where some member of the split supplies inserted bases while consuming a DIFFERENT number of reference bases — a gap-bearing member, the mechanism `:46` states as an inserted sequence "realigning" against the reference. A split whose members are all pure deletions inserts nothing, so `:46`'s mechanism never occurred, and `:17` / `general.md:33` govern unqualified: the members stay individual. This is a further scope on `delins-merge-vs-individual-gap-two-or-more` (payload-coincidence, net-deletion direction) and `delins-payload-coincidence-carve-out-is-coding-dna-scoped` (DNA-axis scope: `c.`/`g.`/`m.`/`n.`, but not the RNA axis); it narrows within those scopes, it does not widen them.

Three things support this reading. First, `:46` states its own mechanism over the INSERTED sequence re-aligning with the reference; a pure-deletion split has no inserted sequence, so `:46` is not describing it. Second, it is the only reading under which both of `:44-47`'s own worked examples come out as the spec writes them: `LRG_199t1:c.850_901delinsTTCCTCGATGCCTG` derives to a split containing a gap-bearing member (consuming 2 reference bases to place 1) and merges, per `:47`; W58's `c.[992_1002del;1004T>C]` derives to three PURE deletions and stays split, though a wide reading would wrongly merge it. Third, it introduces no new constant or threshold — the spec's only stated threshold is on separation (`:81`, at one), and a novel-base-count threshold would be the least-supported reading.

On a genomic axis it does not fire and `delins.md:17` governs unopposed -- members described individually. A projection therefore does not re-merge its derived genomic axis to match a merged coding one.

The grounds are several. `:42`'s antecedent has two conjuncts -- "separated by one nucleotide" AND "together affecting one amino acid." The second is not statable on a genomic reference, so the antecedent is unsatisfied there, not merely weaker. `general.md:22`/`:25` make the `g` prefix a mandatory claim about the reference type (linear genomic), regardless of how gene-scoped the accession is -- `LRG_199:g....` is genomic; `LRG_199t1:c....` is coding -- and there is no `NG_`/`LRG_` carve-out to build from accession alone. The spec restricts by naming prefixes when it means to (`general.md:43` scopes the exon-junction exception to `c./r./n.`), and neither `:18` nor `:42` names a prefix. As inverse precedent, `general.md:42` says the 3' rule applies to "ALL" axes explicitly when it means universal -- the codon carve-out does not say that. And a merged genomic string is not re-derivable from its own reference (which transcript/isoform/strand/frame applies is annotation, often ambiguous), so merging it would make project-then-normalize a non-fixed-point on that axis.

This corrects an over-reading: an earlier reading treated `delins-codon-carve-out-gap-one` (which settles when two variants merge -- gap of one, one amino acid) as also settling which axes the merge reaches. It does not; that record's own applies_to is all `c./r.` strings and its rationale states the carve-out is scoped to the coding sequence.

The scope is narrow: it rules on DNA axes only (`DNA/delins.md`'s own jurisdiction). The `r.` axis merges on `RNA/delins.md:18`'s own authority and is not ruled on here. The `p.` axis is the protein consequence itself. The `n.` axis is not settled: it declares a non-coding reference and carries no frame, yet CDS-offset-derived projection renders it merged while normalizing the `n.` form directly does not merge it -- left open deliberately.

Worth recording as a counterweight: the exception sentence itself carries no axis restriction in its text; the axis reading is inferred from its antecedent, rationale, and worked examples. Of the document set's occurrences of "amino acid," only a minority carry a worked example at all, and every one that does is a `c.` example -- none is `g.`, `n.`, or `m.`, in a document that otherwise uses `g.` freely.
