rulings.question: Is "equivalent inputs produce one canonical output" still the release gate, and what does "equivalent" mean when it cannot be defined by the normalizer the gate is about?

clauses.quote: the 3'rule applies to ALL descriptions (genome, gene, transcript, and protein) of a given variant.
one would end up at the wrong nucleotide, in the wrong exon

`r.123_125[23]` describes a tri-nucleotide repeat of 23 units which **could be interrupted** with other units (e.g., a rare `cua`). The description `r.123cug[23]` can thus only be used when the repeat was sequenced.
First, the two variants may have been reported (or might occur) individually.

rulings.rationale:
The release gate -- equivalent inputs produce one canonical output -- is restated non-circularly: normalize is constant on each equivalence class, where equivalence is apply-equality on every DETERMINED axis (`EquivalenceLevel::CrossAxisSequenceMatch`), never `NormalizedMatch`. It is asserted only over DECIDED pairs; the Indeterminate count is reported alongside and never folded into either side.

It is restated this way because a gate written over "normalizes to the same string" is tautological for any deterministic function and cannot go red. `apply` escapes this -- it maps description to SEQUENCE (byte equality on bases), a codomain independent of ferro's normalizer or any choice this project makes -- so the relation is stated over `apply` while the gate remains over `normalize`, and the two cannot collapse into each other.

One axis is not enough because two descriptions can be apply-equal on the transcript axis they happen to be written in while projecting to different positions, even different exons, on the genome -- the axis a description is spelled in does not by itself establish that two descriptions denote one variant. `general.md:42` (the 3' rule applies to "ALL descriptions -- genome, gene, transcript, and protein") is cited as evidence the spec treats one variant's axes as not independent, not as an equivalence rule itself.

An axis is determined when the description's coordinates carry to it by a mapping that is a function of REFERENCE DATA ALONE (exon alignments, CDS offsets), never of normalization. A `c./n./r.` description determines both the transcript and, via its exon alignment, the genome. A `g./m.` description determines only the genome -- it does not determine a transcript, since many transcripts can overlap one locus and picking one is a choice, not a mapping.

Protein is excluded, and not for cost: translation is many-to-one, so `apply`-agreement on the protein axis is evidence of nothing, and `p.` states a CONSEQUENCE rather than a denotation. Including it would weaken the conjunction in one direction and make it meaningless in the other.

Undecidable is not negative: previously `NotEquivalent` conflated "these denote different sequences" with "no denotation could be computed." `EquivalenceLevel::Indeterminate` separates them; `is_decided()` is what a census reads. A large fraction of previously-`NotEquivalent` pairs are in fact undecidable (uncertain edits/boundaries, multi-molecule alleles, non-literal payloads) -- any confluence figure that does not separate them overstates its denominator.

This does not solve, by design, the case where two descriptions can be apply-equal on every determined axis while making different EPISTEMIC claims about provenance or certainty (e.g. an RNA repeat spelled as an exact unit sequence vs. as an uninterrupted-tract assumption, or a delins vs. two individually-reported variants, `delins.md:83`). That gap is not a missing rung -- adding one would make the relation a function of the input's spelling again, reintroducing the circularity this record removes. It belongs to a ruling about canonical FORM, not to this one.

This settles what "equivalent" means for the gate and that it is stated over decided pairs only. It does not choose which of several conformant forms to converge on (`canonical-form-choice-when-both-legal`); it does not touch the disclosure obligation for confluence fixes that move shipped strings; and it does not resolve `separation-is-a-property-of-the-spelling-not-of-the-variant` (stays undecided).

One tripwire: the genomic re-expression used for cross-axis comparison must never route through the normalizer itself, or the circularity returns and this record is void -- it must stay pure coordinate arithmetic over exon/strand data with no dependency on `normalize`.
rulings.summary: Ferro's release gate asserts that inputs denoting the same sequence on every determined axis, the protein axis excluded, normalize to one output; it is asserted over decided equivalence classes only, and equivalence is judged by applying the descriptions to the reference rather than by comparing normalized strings.

A non-leading lower-case `x` in an `r.` description is refused, mirroring the refusal of alignment-only `X` on the DNA axes. `background/standards.md:47-61` governs: the RNA symbol table lists exactly the DNA table's non-daggered rows (lowercased, `u` for `t`) and has no counterpart at all for either daggered row (`X`, `-`). `general.md:49` requires `r.` nucleotides to use "IUPAC-IUBMB assigned nucleotide symbols," and the RNA table is that assignment — `x` is not in it.

On jurisdiction: a `DNA/` document cannot scope the `r.` axis, but `background/standards.md` carries both symbol tables, so citing its RNA half is an RNA-jurisdiction citation, not a DNA clause stretched across axes.

What is already settled is not re-argued here. `alignment-only-symbol-in-a-description` (decided) already refuses uppercase `X`, including on `r.`; `absolute-prohibition-enforcement-stage` (decided) sets where such refusals live — strict fails at parse, lenient fails only when it cannot normalize, silent is lenient without messages. This record is only about the lower-case `r.`-axis spelling.

This is live, not cosmetic. The parser dispatches an inserted sequence on its content, and a single stray `x` byte reclassifies an otherwise-literal nucleotide run wholesale into a mobile-element name — accepted and re-emitted byte-identically in every error mode with no warning. Normalization is not merely permissive there, it is vacuous: the output looks normalized while carrying a spelling `general.md:49` does not admit.

One reading is rejected: absence from the RNA table might read as silence rather than prohibition, since the dagger marking alignment-only symbols is explicit and sits only in the DNA table. That reading is rejected because `general.md:49` names the IUPAC-IUBMB table as the source of legal symbols, not merely a style guide — the RNA table's silence is exclusion, not permission.

The scope is symbol-specific, not an alphabet-wide rule — lower-case `x` on the DNA axes is unchanged. A leading `x` (or lone `x`) is already refused by the grammar in every mode regardless of this ruling; only a non-leading `x` is mode-dependent, per `absolute-prohibition-enforcement-stage`. A named-element payload not spelled with `x` (e.g. `Named("alu")`) is untouched — this keys on the symbol, not on whether the payload is a nucleotide run.

The accepted cost: an `r.` insert naming a mobile element whose name contains a non-leading lower-case `x` is now refused. No such name is known to occur in the corpus, the spec, or the fixtures.

rulings.question: A `c.`/`n.` position is written against a transcript accession whose cdot exon table has a transcript-coordinate gap. Does it name the base at that offset in the flat transcript sequence, or the base reached by walking the exon table across the gap?

clauses.quote: numbering starts with `c.1` at the **`A`** of the `ATG` translation initiation (start) codon and ends with the last nucleotide of the translation termination (stop) codon
nucleotide numbering is `n.1`, `n.2`, `n.3`, ..., etc., from the first to the last nucleotide of the reference sequence.
a coding DNA reference sequence **does not contain** intron or 5' and 3' gene flanking sequences, and can therefore **not be used as a reference** to describe variants in these regions
it is **not** allowed to describe variants in nucleotides beyond the boundaries of a transcript reference sequence, using that transcript reference sequence.

rulings.rationale:
A c./n. position names the base at that offset in the transcript's FLAT sequence and must never be resolved by walking the exon table. This decides against CoordinateMapper's cds_to_tx/tx_to_cds, which walked cdot's exon list and added any gap in it to positions 3' of the gap while ReferenceProvider kept serving the flat transcript — so hgvs_to_spdi and the normalizer named different bases of the same accession.

numbering.md:52 defines n. numbering as consecutive (n.1, n.2, ...) "from the first to the last nucleotide of the reference sequence" — a count over the sequence's own nucleotides, with no term for an alignment; :21 ties c. to the same count, re-origined at the start codon. Neither mentions a genome or an exon. :40 (a coding reference excludes introns/flanking) and :44 (no positions beyond transcript bounds) are supporting context only, not authority: :40 is about introns/flanking, not about unaligned-but-present transcript bases, and :44 isn't engaged since the positions at issue are well inside the transcript.

The gap case is moot, not unanswered: numbering is defined over the reference sequence's own bases; alignment to a genome is not a term in that definition, so a gap in the alignment cannot produce a gap in the numbering — the exon walk answers a different question ("how far along the genome alignment is this?") than what a c./n. number asks. Some cdot builds do carry genuine (always in-frame) transcript-to-genome alignment gaps; the ruling doesn't rest on their being rare, but on whose coordinate space a gap is in — it is a fact about the transcript's genome alignment, not about the accession's own numbering, which RefSeq's own annotation (protein length, CDS extent, contiguous exon table) counts straight through.

A separate defect, noted but not decided here: cdot's own codon coordinates are gap-collapsed while its exon tx coordinates are flat — two different spaces within cdot itself — and ferro's cdot loader copies the gap-collapsed codon coordinates into a flat-space field, so the live provider can under-report cds_end by the gap size. This ruling isolates that provider-resolution defect but does not fix it.

In scope is the sequence frame only (c./n. <-> transcript). The genome frame — mapping a transcript position to/from a contig — stays exon- and CIGAR-aware and unchanged; a gap there still correctly means "this transcript base aligns to nothing" (reported as None, never as a shifted coordinate). Same principle as the already-decided CIGAR-insertion case (a CIGAR insertion adds transcript bases absent from the genome, and c. already counts them) — this ruling brings CoordinateMapper into line with that same principle.

This is not decided by consulting Mutalyzer: it is settled at adjudication-precedence-order's first rank (spec-explicit) before Mutalyzer is even consulted; it is also not probative here by construction, since it resolves positions against its own reference retrieval rather than cdot's genome alignment.

The representation impact is confined to transcripts whose cdot exon table has a gap — every c./n. position 3' of the gap, and every SPDI/applied base derived from it, moves by the gap size, toward the base the accession's own numbering names. Gap-free transcripts are unaffected.
rulings.summary: A 'c.'/'n.' position names the base at that offset in the flat transcript sequence and is never resolved by walking the exon table, so it lands correctly even on a transcript whose cdot alignment carries a gap.

The test applies to each piece of the partition ferro derives from the resulting sequence -- a piece whose payload is not a copy of the reference bases immediately 5' of its insertion point is not a duplication, and `:18` never fires on it.

The grounds for this are independent and both load-bearing -- a single lowercase-prose clause is weak authority per `exon-junction-dup-converge-from-the-far-side`'s calibration:
1. `:17` is the parent clause fixing when the `dup` label may be used at all; `:18`/`:19`/`:20` are its sub-bullets and all three swap ONE LABEL FOR ANOTHER over the SAME span -- none says "and not as, e.g., two members." The MUST ranks a label inside a scope the parent fixes.
2. `:18`'s subject, "a variant," is defined in `background/glossary.md:310-311` as a difference between reference and observed sequence -- a property of the pair, prior to any partition. `general.md:55`/`:56` (`:18`'s own cited authority) rank single-variant type labels for one span and never rank a multi-member allele against a spanning description (`adjudication-precedence-order`, escalation E1).

This extends to net-longer duplications: when the resulting sequence carries a NET-LONGER, clean tandem copy-number change of a MULTI-BASE reference motif (anchored 5' or 3'-shiftable), the derivation partitions to expose that `dup` rather than let the coarser solid-run collapse merge it away. A single-base shift-anchor is excluded -- that is the solid-run collapse, not a duplication (the discriminator is a two-or-more-base motif, never a reference tandem-copy floor). Scoped to exactly one reference-tandem dup beside exactly one substitution; widening past that regresses forms the spec prefers merged (a dup beside a deletion or an insertion, or two insertions at one junction, stay merged -- other records' territory).

This narrows for the net-zero case, though not the net-longer one: an EQUAL-LENGTH, all-differing run where a coincidence lets the minimal alignment spell part of it as dup+del does NOT get this treatment -- nothing was actually duplicated, so partitioning to manufacture a `dup` there violates this record's own LABEL-NOT-PARTITION principle. Such runs collapse to the spanning delins instead (`delins.md:16`, `:44-47`; `general.md:57` forbids the `[del;dup]` shape by name). The net-shorter direction needs no such guard -- it already renders as a spanning delins with no outside-anchored dup.

Left open and recorded as unanswered: whether a spec MUST binds here is decided partly by how coarsely the derivation cuts -- set by a window constant and by whether an unrelated third member falls inside it, so the same sequence change can be dup-bearing or not depending on distance from an unrelated edit. The reply on offer is that this indicts the partitioner's locality, not the reading; that reply is recorded as a reply, not as settling the objection.

This is a PREFERENCE among conformant forms, not a conformance fix -- both the dup-exposing and the merged spellings are legal. It moves shipped output only where the coalescing/solid-run machinery would otherwise have merged a genuine net-longer tandem dup away, or where a net-zero dup+del coincidence is now collapsed to delins instead.

rulings.rationale:
A `c.` description against a transcript reference whose CDS start ferro cannot resolve is refused rather than normalized or returned unchanged -- there is no origin to number the coordinate from.

This is governed by `numbering.md:21` -- `c.` numbering starts at the `A` of the ATG start codon, so a `c.` number is defined by that codon's position; when nothing in the reference locates it, the number does not name an identifiable base. `refseq.md:129` adds that a `c.` reference sequence "includes the CDS and the 5'/3' UTR regions"; a record with no located CDS is not being used as one in that sense.

This is a house choice rather than a clause ruling (rule 6, disclosed under rule 7): the recommendations describe descriptions, not what a tool must do when it cannot find the codon. Returning the input unchanged and refusing are both conformant; refusing was chosen because, per settled precedent (`canonical-form-choice-when-both-legal` and the `from_sequences` refusal policy), ferro refuses visibly rather than pick or fabricate when it lacks the information or authority to choose. The prior behavior -- silent identity pass-through, `status: ok`, `changed: false` -- let distinct spellings of one variant on such a transcript normalize to distinct strings (breaking caller dedup) and let out-of-bounds positions through unchecked.

The refusal happens at normalize, not at parse. This differs from `absolute-prohibition-enforcement-stage`, whose subject is input conformance -- a fact about the string, decidable without a reference. Here the string is perfectly conformant; what fails is the reference's ability to resolve it, a fact that changes with the reference version and that `parse_hgvs` (holding no provider) cannot see at all.

It applies unconditionally across strict/lenient/silent -- not a new mode policy but falls directly out of the existing one. Lenient's contract is "fails only if it cannot normalize"; ferro has no origin to number from, so lenient's own stated behavior is to fail, and silent fails without a message. No per-mode override or per-code exception applies, for the same reason others like it may not.

The scope is a transcript reference serving bases but resolving no CDS. A bare genomic parent (`NG_`/`NC_`/`LRG_` with no transcript-selector resolved) is not this -- its `c.` names an implied transcript, and resolving that implication is the legacy-gene-selector machinery's job, not this ruling's; the check is scoped so it does not fire on that record and reject a question nobody asked.

Untouched are `n.` (counts over the reference's own nucleotides, needs no CDS, keeps working on the same accessions this refuses) and `p.` (already refused through `project`). Not settled: the `r.` axis, which deliberately numbers the transcript even with no resolved CDS -- a separate question; whether the reference should resolve these CDSs (a degraded-artifact problem, tracked separately); and a record carrying `cds_start` but not `cds_end`.

Worth recording rather than arguing away: the spec's own minus-strand worked example (`refseq.md:145`) uses `NM_004006.1:c.5697del`, a transcript version in exactly this class -- that row now errors on ferro's spec corpus. This does not defeat the ruling: the refusal is about the reference ferro holds, not the description (the same string normalizes against a CDS-bearing version), and ferro's `project` surface already refused this same row before this change -- `normalize` is joining `project`, closing a prior internal contradiction (one binary, one input, two exit codes) rather than newly rejecting a spec example.
rulings.summary: A 'c.' description against a transcript whose CDS start the reference cannot resolve is refused rather than returned unchanged, because ferro has no origin to number the coordinate from.

house_choice.considered_and_rejected: Four readings were weighed and put aside, and the first is the one that matters because it is the reading this record replaced. THE POSITION-WISE READING — pair column i of the reference against column i of the observed. Rejected, but NOT because a clause forbids it: it has no less textual support than the minimal-alignment reading, and no more. It is rejected because it is not stable under the thing it is supposed to describe — on an equal-length block it reports changed columns that a cheaper alignment leaves untouched, so two spellings of one variant can present different separations and `general.md:34` then returns two answers for one variant. `rulings[derivation-may-not-be-bounded-by-the-inputs-spelling]` records four rows where exactly that happened. READING `general.md:34` AS ITSELF SUPPLYING THE PROCEDURE. Rejected on measurement rather than on argument, so the measurement is stated with the command that produced it and with the checkout it was run at. In the pinned submodule at `565b973`: `git grep -n -i -E 'minimal|minimum' -- docs/recommendations docs/background docs/consultation`. Over those three trees `cost` is 0, `parsimon*` 0, `edit distance` 0, `optimal` 0, `fewest` 0, and there are SEVEN `minimal`/`minimum` hits, all seven in `docs/recommendations/` and none in `docs/background/` or `docs/consultation/`. They fall into three groups, and the third is the one an earlier draft of this paragraph mis-filed: the extent of an unsequenced deletion or duplication (`uncertain.md:33`, `:159`); SNP-array probe bounds (`DNA/deletion.md:100`, `DNA/duplication.md:106`); and one notational character-economy note — 'the recommendations try to restrict the number of different characters used to a minimum' — repeated verbatim on all three axes (`DNA/insertion.md:106`, `RNA/insertion.md:62`, `protein/insertion.md:73`). That third group is the closest thing in the corpus to the concept being disclaimed and it is notational, not operational. None of the seven edits minimality, so the conclusion is unchanged; what changed is the arithmetic, which in a paragraph resting on measurement is not a detail. SEVEN IS NOT AN ARTEFACT OF HOW THE SCAN IS DRAWN: case-sensitive and case-insensitive agree, per-line and per-occurrence agree, adding word boundaries agrees (checked under `perl`, because `git grep -E` does not honour `\b` and silently returns 0 for it), and restricting to `*.md` agrees; the only `minim*` forms present anywhere in the three trees are `minimal` twice and `minimum` five times. The count is also unchanged from the `6f85311` checkout this paragraph was first measured at — all seven line anchors survived the bump to `565b973` unmoved. There is no definition of `unchanged` for a block differing at several positions, and no procedure of any kind for deriving a partition from two sequences. `:34` raises the question and does not answer it. PROVENANCE-BASED INDIVIDUATION, which appears to be the spec's own model — `DNA/delins.md:81-84` grounds the split-by-default rule in the two variants having 'been reported (or might occur) individually', and `DNA/complex.md:12` says HGVS describes 'the variant(s) detected'. Rejected as unavailable rather than as wrong: a normalizer holds a reference and an observed sequence and no report, so it cannot recover provenance. `rulings[separation-is-a-property-of-the-spelling-not-of-the-variant]` already records that deviation. COUNTER-EVIDENCE, RECORDED UNRESOLVED. `DNA/delins.md:44-47` is the corpus's only worked confrontation with alignment-derived splitting and it prefers the COARSER form, calling the split 'an alternative description' and recommending the spanning `delins` on two stated grounds; `:46` puts the word 'align' in the committee's own scare quotes; and `DNA/delins.md:86-89` records a second case where permission for a split spelling was WITHDRAWN. Two existing records scope `:47` away from the blocks this rule governs — `delins-payload-coincidence-carve-out-is-coding-dna-scoped` to the `c.` axis and `delins-merge-vs-individual-gap-two-or-more` to the net-deletion direction — so the passage does not currently reach them, but that is a consequence of those scopes and not a refutation of the counter-evidence. REVISITED 2026-08-15, AND BOTH SCOPES HOLD. `delins.md:86-89` is a CODING-axis, net-INSERTION, separation-ZERO case already ruled on by `delins-adjacent-members-when-both-consume-reference`, so it reaches neither scope; and it was in front of the operator when both were written, `c0742311` having brought it into the ledger 52 minutes before the axis scope landed. Widening the axis is blocked rather than merely unattractive: a frameless two-member split at separation one falls inside `spec_corpus::is_svd_wg010_shape`, which `guard_violations` pins at zero over 210 rows as a verdict on the rejected proposal. rulings.question: `general.md:33` keys on variants 'separated by one or more nucleotides' and `DNA/delins.md:16` on 'two or more consecutive nucleotides'. Both quantify over nucleotides being unchanged or changed, and neither names an alignment. Against WHICH alignment is a reference base judged unchanged — the position-wise correspondence available when the two sides are the same length, or the minimal-edit alignment?

clauses.quote: two variants separated by one or more nucleotides should be described individually and **not** as a "delins"
changes involving two or more consecutive nucleotides are described as deletion/insertion (delins) variants
changes involving two or more consecutive nucleotides are described as deletion-insertion (delins) so the description
The recommendations for the description of sequence variants are designed to be **stable**, **meaningful**, **memorable**, and **unequivocal**

rulings.rationale:
A reference base is unchanged iff it is matched in EVERY minimal alignment of the block — a column-based notion, not cell-based, not position-wise — and this is a house choice with no governing clause. `general.md:33`'s "separated by one or more nucleotides" and `delins.md:16`'s "two or more consecutive nucleotides" are evaluated against that notion. The recommendations raise the question of what "unchanged"/"separated" means but supply no procedure for answering it — they neither require nor forbid this reading, so it carries no governing clause and is never citable as conformance (ruleset rule 5 silent limb).

This rules out treating a block as necessarily equal-length-and-unchanged: a block can be equal length and still contain an indel under the minimal alignment (e.g. a balanced del+ins pair reads as two separated changes with unchanged bases between them, even though a position-wise column-by-column reading would show every column differing). Treating such a split as an "artifact" of choosing a del+ins decomposition, and citing `delins.md:16`/`substitution.md:32` to force it back into one spanning change, is wrong: the position-wise pairing is the reading with no authority behind it, not the minimal alignment.

An operator-ratified exception supersedes the general rule for one shape only: where a block is an EQUAL-LENGTH run with NO interior zero-shift fixed point — no base surviving at its own coordinate, every position-wise column differing — it collapses to one spanning `delins` instead (e.g. `CAG->AGA` is `delinsAGA`, not split). There the minimal-alignment interior matches are shift artifacts, not separators. This restores the pre-v0.14.0 position-wise reading for that shape on top of the `canonical-coalesced` default. The `dup` MUST (`duplication.md:18`, see `duplication-must-ranks-the-label-not-the-partition`) overrides this collapse only when a member duplicates a MULTI-BASE reference motif; a single-base shift-anchor does not count and stays collapsed.

The cost model is not fixed, though: "minimal" presupposes a cost model, and two candidates disagree on which bases are unchanged for some blocks — unit-cost substitution vs. substitution-as-delete-plus-insert (cost 2). Evidence favors unit-cost substitution, but this is not a ruling — do not cite this record for a case where the two models differ without saying which was used. (The equal-length-collapse exception above moots the divergence for any block with no interior fixed point, since there is no interior unchanged set left to disagree over.)

This is a factual test for which bases are unchanged, not a minimality principle for preferring a shorter description — which of several legal descriptions ships is governed separately by `derivation-may-not-be-bounded-by-the-inputs-spelling` and `canonical-form-choice-when-both-legal`.
rulings.summary: Ferro treats a reference base as unchanged only when every minimum-edit alignment of the block matches it — a project choice the recommendations neither require nor forbid — except that an equal-length run with no base surviving at its own coordinate is rendered as one spanning delins.

rulings.question: A span whose whole content is replaced by its exact reverse complement always admits a competing partition at the columns where the complement coincides with the reference. `inversion-vs-two-delins-76-83` typed the span `inv` because that partition was two `delins`, which `general.md:55` does not rank; #1230 split the span because that partition was substitutions, which `:55` ranks above inversion. Does the TYPE of the competing partition decide the typing, or does the span?

clauses.quote: a sequence change where, compared to a reference sequence, **more than one nucleotide** replacing the original sequence is the reverse complement of the original sequence
a one-nucleotide inversion should be described as a [substitution](substitution.md)

**`NM_004006.2:c.4145_4160inv`**
inversion of the 16 nucleotides from position `c.4145` to `c.4160`.
two variants separated by one or more nucleotides should be described individually and **not** as a "delins"
the preferred description is: (1) substitution, (2) deletion, (3) inversion, (4) duplication, (5) insertion
one or more nucleotides are replaced by one or more other nucleotides **and which is not** a substitution or inversion
changes involving two or more consecutive nucleotides are described as deletion-insertion (delins) so the description c.[79G>T;80C>T] is not correct
are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119]

rulings.rationale:
A span whose entire content is the exact reverse complement of the reference is typed `inv`, uniformly — however much of the interior happens to coincide with the reference, and whatever the competing multi-member partition would be. Test: `block == revcomp(block)` over the trimmed block, evaluated on the resulting sequence; this settles the typing before any cut is considered. `inversion.md:5` governs, being the clause that states the property, stated over the whole span.

As for why the reach of the neighboring clauses doesn't decide this: `general.md:55` ranks single-variant type labels for one span; it does not reach a contest between a whole-span `inv` and a multi-member allele (`adjudication-precedence-order` escalation E1), so it cannot decide this either way — the ranking is real but out of scope, not refuted. `general.md:33`'s separation preference is rule 2 (a preference, not a compulsion), and in any case a one-variant span has no "two variants" to separate. `substitution.md:32` prohibits adjacent members; it does not require a split at a gap. `inversion.md:16` only redirects the degenerate one-nucleotide case to a substitution.

This is corroborated by the spec's own worked example (`inversion.md:33-34`, `NM_004006.2:c.4145_4160inv`), which has two self-complementary interior runs and is still called `inv` outright — spec silence would have been weaker; this is a worked case. Mutalyzer independently returns the whole-span `inv` on every probed locus, both against substitution and against delins competitors, but is corroboration only, never authority (`adjudication-precedence-order`).

This sits in the ruleset's rule 6 ("among multiple conformant forms, the maintainers choose") plus rule 7 disclosure — no clause COMPELS the `inv` spelling; the split forms are also conformant. Do not cite this as a rule-1 correctness fix.

One counterweight stays unanswered: `general.md:55` does rank substitution above inversion; what retires it here is that E1 puts this contest outside its scope, not a refutation of the ranking itself. There is also no length or density bound on how much interior coincidence is tolerated before typing as `inv` — a coincidence fraction only proxies for span length, and any future bound would need its own ruling.

One caveat: a guard once read a long inversion's re-derived multi-member competitor as violating `substitution.md:32`'s ban on adjacent members; the adjacent pairs it found all flank `ins` members (which consume no reference), not two substitutions, so `:32`'s named shape does not occur there — don't cite that guard's finding with its original attribution.

This reaches only spans whose whole content is an exact reverse complement; the competing partition governs unchanged for any other span. It says nothing about where such a span's boundaries fall (trimming/shifting/hull selection untouched), and does not reach `delins-adjacent-members-when-both-consume-reference` or `duplication-must-ranks-the-label-not-the-partition`. It supersedes the competitor-type distinction drawn in `inversion-vs-two-delins-76-83` and subsumes `inversion-vs-a-mixed-member-competitor`; their outcomes stand, their stated reasoning is replaced by this record. It moves output for every currently-split whole-span-reverse-complement case; disclose as a representation change (rule 7).
rulings.summary: A span whose whole content is replaced by its exact reverse complement is written as one inv, however much of its interior coincides with the reference and whatever the competing partition is made of; this is a project choice among conformant forms, not a conformance requirement.

rulings.question: On an unequal-length changed block, ferro's partitioner cuts at the one column where a payload base coincides with a reference base and emits the residual gap as a member of its own. Do `general.md:34` / `DNA/delins.md:17` govern the members that cut produces, or does `DNA/delins.md:47` recommend the spanning `delins`?

clauses.quote: parts of the inserted sequence "align" with the reference sequence, giving an alternative description like `c.[850_869del;874_881del;887_897del;901_902insG]`
**The "delins" format is recommended**
two variants separated by one or more nucleotides should be described individually and **not** as a "delins"
two variants separated by one or more nucleotides should be described individually and **not** as a "delins"
one variant can be described using different formats. This is undesired; HGVS recommendations should be extended by specifying when to use which format.

rulings.rationale:
A lone unequal-length net-deletion delins whose payload merely coincides with the reference at the gap alignment placed, and whose every other member would itself render as a delins, is kept whole rather than split at that coincidence -- on every DNA axis (`c.`, `g.`, `m.`, `n.`); not on `r.`, which is outside a DNA clause's jurisdiction (`RNA/delins.md` states no counterpart to `:47`).

This is governed by `docs/recommendations/DNA/delins.md:47`, the spec's stated preference for the span form; `:46` describes the construction it prefers over. Neither form is prohibited -- this is a rule-6 choice among conformant forms, not a conformance requirement, and must never be cited as such.

The ground: `general.md:33` and `DNA/delins.md:17` require an established separation between two variants. On an unequal-length block that separation is not established by the sequences -- it is manufactured by whichever column-alignment the partitioner happened to pick, and the spec does not say which alignment to choose. Recovering a decomposition means choosing among alignments with no derivable answer, so `:47`'s span preference is what settles it.

Four conditions narrow the scope, each one further:
1. NET DELETION only -- a payload shorter than its span. Net insertions are not reached.
2. Every inter-member separation is exactly one unchanged base -- real distance between members (more than one unchanged base) stays split.
3. Some member supplies bases that force the realignment -- a split that inserts nothing is not an artifact of this mechanism and stays split.
4. Every other member, considered alone, would render as a delins -- not a substitution, inversion, or duplication, each of which is a real type the split buys and each of which stays split. This includes a pure deletion member: where the deleted span is only the gap an aligner placed, it is not a real deletion the sequences separated out, and is folded in; this is the one condition this ruling changed from prior (narrower) practice, which had declined to fold in as soon as any member was a pure deletion.

The axis scope is gated on the same carve-out predicate as `delins-payload-coincidence-carve-out-is-coding-dna-scoped` (`CoincidenceCarveOut::may_disbelieve_a_separation`); this rule inherits that predicate's axis reach rather than keeping a private copy, so any later change to the carve-out's scope moves this rule's reach automatically. Currently: all DNA axes, not `r.`.

One caveat: a block containing a genuine substitution, inversion, or duplication member (condition 4) is unaffected and stays split -- this rule only folds in a placed gap, never a real type.
rulings.summary: A lone unequal-length net-deletion delins whose payload merely coincides with the reference, and whose every member other than the placed gap would itself render as a delins, is kept whole on every DNA axis (c./g./m./n., but not r.) rather than split at that coincidence into a separate residual member.

rulings.question: `DNA/inversion.md:69` recommends that an inverted duplication be described `ins<range>inv`, naming the span the inverted copy was taken from. Ferro expanded such a payload to reverse-complemented literal bases and never derived the recommended form. Is emitting the literal a defect, or a free choice between two legal spellings — and if the form is to be derived, what stops a short reverse-complement coincidence from being mis-read as an inverted duplication, given that the spec supplies no minimum length for one?

clauses.quote: the recommendation is to describe inverted duplication using the format `g.122_123ins123_234inv` or `g.234_235ins123_234inv` depending on whether the inverted copy is 5' or 3' of the original copy
a sequence change where, compared to a reference sequence, **more than one nucleotide** replacing the original sequence is the reverse complement of the original sequence
a copy of one or more nucleotides is inserted **directly 3'** of the original copy of that sequence
the preferred description is: (1) substitution, (2) deletion, (3) inversion, (4) duplication, (5) insertion
**inverted duplications** are described as an insertion (`r.234_235ins123_234inv`), not as a duplication

rulings.rationale:
This is an operator ruling, dated 2026-08-14, a DEFECT fix rather than a free choice. An inverted duplication is derived as `ins<range>inv` (naming the source span, inverted), not expanded to literal reverse-complemented bases. `inversion.md:69` ("the recommendation is") governs and is restated as a Note in five further places (`DNA/insertion.md:18`, `DNA/duplication.md:20`, `DNA/inversion.md:19`, `RNA/insertion.md:18`, `RNA/duplication.md:21`), each rejecting the `dupinv` shorthand. It is not a `canonical-form-choice-when-both-legal` question, because a clause selects the form by name; it mirrors the uninverted case, which ferro already re-spells `dup`.

The coincidence floor is house policy — cite nothing for it. A payload matches a neighbour's reverse complement by chance often, so deriving `ins<range>inv` from any match would mint spurious inverted duplications. The spec supplies no minimum; only `inversion.md:5`'s "more than one nucleotide" applies, excluding a one-base payload definitionally. The floor is composition-aware, not a length cutoff: it fires only when the payload is at least two bases, is not self-complementary (a self-complementary payload is a duplication — `general.md:56` ranks duplication above insertion), and has a chance-match probability under the local base composition at or below threshold. The composition is read over a fixed window (`COMPOSITION_HALF_WIDTH`), not the caller's `NormalizeConfig::window_size`, so the emitted form does not depend on a config knob; the threshold is an order of magnitude (~1e-5), and the decline/fire boundary rather than the constant is what is pinned.

RNA is in scope on its own authority (`RNA/insertion.md:18`, `RNA/duplication.md:21`), not by stretching a `DNA/` clause. It is WIRED ONLY in `normalize_genome` today, so `c.`/`n.`/`r.`/`m.` still emit literals and one inverted duplication spells differently per axis — the largest known gap; the long-term home is a render stage seeing the final member list. The derived form and its literal resolve to the SAME SPDI (a provider is required, so the no-provider paths decline as they do for the short forms), and the VCF converter now DECLINES a range payload it cannot spell as bases rather than emit an HGVS spelling into the ALT field.

This moves rows in representation terms: any stored description whose payload is the reverse complement of its abutting span, at or above the floor, re-spells to `ins<range>inv`. Pinned by `tests/it/recommended_form_pins.rs::the_coincidence_floor_sits_between_eight_and_nine_bases`, `tests/it/recommended_form_pins.rs::the_derived_range_form_and_its_literal_resolve_to_the_same_spdi`, and `tests/it/issue_390_hgvs_vcf_provider_coverage.rs::range_payload_never_reaches_alt`.
rulings.summary: An inverted duplication is written as 'ins<range>inv', naming the span the inverted copy came from, rather than expanded to reverse-complemented literal bases; whether a payload counts as an inverted copy at all is gated by a house coincidence-probability floor, not any spec-stated minimum — and it is wired today only in normalize_genome, so c./n./r./m. still emit literals.

rulings.question: On the HGVS→SPDI conversion path, should an `N`-unit (or `N`-containing) repeat be REFUSED, or expanded into the SPDI `insertion` string as a run of literal `N`s? `insN[341]` currently emits 341 `N`s even though `N[341]` carries a length, not bases — the same information content as the length-only `ins341` shape SPDI already refuses (#1967).

house_choice.considered_and_rejected:
EMITTING THE `N`-RUN (the status quo this record replaces). Rejected: `insN[341]` produced 341 literal `N`s in the SPDI `insertion` field — a well-formed triple a consumer can store and key read counts on, asserting 341 specific bases the input never named. `N[341]` carries a length, not bases, so it is the exact information content of `ins341` (`InsertedSequence::Count`), which SPDI already refuses (#1967); emitting one while refusing the other treats equally-undetermined inputs inconsistently. #1747 settles the direction: `c.pterdel`/`c.qterdel`/`c.1del` all produced a storable-but-wrong SPDI triple and were refused, on the principle that a plausible-but-wrong answer a consumer can persist is worse than a clean decline.

CLASSIFYING IT AS `MissingReferenceData`. Rejected: nothing is missing and no provider can supply the identity of an `N`, because the input declines to name it. `UnrepresentableInSpdi` is the variant whose contract is 'decided from the description alone, and no better-provisioned provider changes the answer' — exactly this case.

RULING IT AS A SPEC-CLAUSE DECISION (a `governing` clause). Rejected: the HGVS recommendations govern HGVS descriptions and say nothing about SPDI, which is NCBI's format. `N` is a legal HGVS symbol (`general.md:47`, IUPAC-IUBMB); the problem is only that SPDI's `insertion` string is concrete DNA bases. So there is no clause to hold governing — this is `normalization-rules.md` rule 5's silent limb, and an SPDI-side `N` representation would be an upstream feature request, not a bug report.

REFUSING CONCRETE-BASE REPEATS TOO (over-reach). Rejected: a concrete unit (`insACGT[3]`, `insA[10]`) names its bases exactly and expands to a determinate, correct SPDI triple, so it must keep emitting. Only undetermined content — an `N` anywhere in the unit — refuses.

clauses.quote: A, C, G or T
nucleotides in CAPITALS using [IUPAC-IUBMB assigned nucleotide symbols]

rulings.rationale:
This is a house choice with no governing clause: on the HGVS-to-SPDI path, ferro refuses an `N`-unit or `N`-containing repeat (`insN[18]`, `delinsN[341]`, the multi-base `insAN[3]`) with `UnrepresentableInSpdi`, rather than expand it into literal `N` bases.

`N` denotes "any of A, C, G or T" (`background/standards.md:30`), so an `N`-repeat states a LENGTH with no base identity — the same information content as the length-only `ins<length>` shape that SPDI conversion already refuses. Expanding it would assert specific bases the input never specified, producing a well-formed but wrong SPDI triple; a clean decline is preferred to a plausible-but-wrong answer (same principle as the `c.pterdel`/`c.qterdel`/`c.1del` refusals).

It is a house choice because the recommendations do not reach SPDI conversion, and `N` is a legal HGVS symbol (`general.md:47`), so no clause governs this; it falls under `normalization-rules.md` rule 5's silent limb.

The guard sits at the shared expansion leaf (top-level `insN[n]`/`delinsN[n]` and the single-part/bracket `Complex` shapes) and at the short-form `NaEdit::Repeat` arm (`g.pos_posN[n]`), decided from the description alone before any reference read. A concrete-base repeat (`insACGT[3]`, `insA[10]`) is untouched — only undetermined content refuses. This is on the HGVS→SPDI conversion path only; no normalized HGVS string moves.
rulings.summary: On the HGVS-to-SPDI path ferro refuses an 'N'-unit or 'N'-containing repeat rather than expand it to literal 'N' bases — a project choice, since 'N' states a length, not identified bases, and the recommendations do not reach SPDI conversion.

rulings.question: A `c.N` coordinate with N greater than `cds_end` (e.g. `c.22` on a transcript whose CDS ends at `c.21`) names no base the coding axis defines. Ferro refused it in strict mode when it stood alone (`c.22del` -> W4004) but silently accepted and remapped it to `*1` inside a cis allele (`c.[22_23insG;*1G>A]` -> `c.21dup`). Which stage owns the refusal, and does the allele path get the same rule as the lone position?

clauses.quote: numbering starts with `c.1` at the **`A`** of the `ATG` translation initiation (start) codon and ends with the last nucleotide of the translation termination (stop) codon
nucleotides downstream (3') of the translation termination codon (stop) are marked with a `*` (asterisk) and numbered `c.*1`, `c.*2`, `c.*3`, etc., going further downstream

rulings.rationale:
A plain `c.N` coordinate with N greater than `cds_end` is a NON-CONFORMANT coordinate, not an alternate spelling of `*(N - cds_end)`.

This is governed by `numbering.md:21`, which ends the coding-DNA axis at the last nucleotide of the stop codon; `:30` opens a separate `c.*` zone the moment the stop codon ends. So `c.22` on a transcript whose CDS ends at `c.21` names no base the `c.` axis defines -- the base one past the stop is spelled `c.*1`, and `c.22` is out-of-scheme numbering for it, not a second name for it.

Enforcement is mode-dependent, applied identically whether the coordinate is a lone position or a member of a cis allele. Strict validates conformance and REFUSES (`W4004 PositionPastEnd`). Lenient does not validate conformance and instead REPAIRS the coordinate to its canonical `c.*(N - cds_end)` spelling, disclosed via the same `W4004` kept in the warning vector rather than silently remapped. Silent is lenient with the message suppressed. Output in the permissive modes is unchanged (it was already the repaired `*N` form); what changes is that the repair is now disclosed, and that strict refuses. The cis-allele path previously reached its equivalent sequence coordinate through a different route that carried no diagnostic -- fixed so both paths run one rule through one gate, so a raw allele member gets `W4004` before any merge reinterprets it.

This is refused at normalize, not parse, for the same reasoning as `c-description-against-an-unresolvable-cds-is-refused`: the input's spelling is conformant: whether `c.22` is in range is a REFERENCE fact (depends on `cds_end`), which parsing holds no provider to see.

The `n.` axis is untouched (a bare `n.` number is a flat offset with no CDS). The 5'UTR (`c.-N`) and 3'UTR (`c.*N`) bound checks ride the same gate and are unchanged. The whole-transcript bound (`:44`) is separate and not engaged by a coordinate landing inside the 3'UTR.

In terms of representation impact: strict newly refuses cis alleles carrying a past-`cds_end` `c.` member that it previously remapped and normalized silently; lenient/silent move no output but now disclose the correction as `W4004`. The lone-position path is unchanged.
rulings.summary: A 'c.N' coordinate past the CDS end is non-conformant: strict mode refuses it, while lenient and silent modes repair it to the equivalent 'c.*' position — applied the same way to a lone position and to a member of a cis allele.

rulings.question: A `c.?` position states that the coordinate is unknown. When `CoordinateMapper::cds_to_tx` converts it toward a transcript coordinate (on the way to SPDI), should it coerce `c.?` into a concrete transcript position, or refuse it? Ferro used to coerce: `c.?` answered `c.1`'s own transcript coordinate (base 6 on the test transcript, which #1910 measured as bit-identical to `c.1+5`), because `CDS_BASE_UNKNOWN` is the integer `0` and `0 < 1` took the 5'UTR branch with a zero displacement.

house_choice.considered_and_rejected:
COERCING `c.?` TO A CONCRETE POSITION (the status quo this record replaces). Rejected: `?` is the spec's explicit marker for an UNKNOWN position (`general.md:87`), so an input carrying it has DECLINED to name the coordinate. `cds_to_tx` answered `c.1`'s own transcript coordinate anyway — a fabricated position, bit-identical to an ordinary in-CDS coordinate — so a description stating "I do not know the position" became a description stating position 6, and through `hgvs_to_spdi` a storable-but-wrong SPDI triple a consumer can persist and key on. That is the same failure the #1747 refusals (`c.pterdel`/`c.qterdel`/`c.1del`, storable-but-wrong triples) and the `spdi-n-unit-repeat-refusal` (`insN[341]`, a length asserted as bases) were decided against: a plausible-but-wrong answer a consumer can persist is worse than a clean decline.

RULING IT AS A SPEC-CLAUSE DECISION (a `governing` clause). Rejected: the recommendations define what `?` MEANS in a description (`general.md:87`, `uncertain.md:12` — an unknown nucleotide or amino acid position) but say nothing about coordinate conversion or about what a tool must do when asked to place `c.?` on a transcript axis. Propagating the `?` through conversion and refusing at conversion are both consistent with the description's meaning; no clause forces the choice. So there is no clause to hold governing — this is `normalization-rules.md` rule 5's silent limb.

DISTINGUISHING IT FROM THE TWO ADJACENT REFERENCE-FRAME RECORDS, because it is easy to file under either and it belongs under neither. `c-and-n-positions-are-flat-transcript-offsets` decides the coordinate SPACE a known `c.` number lives in (flat offset vs. exon walk); `c.?` carries no number to place in any space. `c-description-against-an-unresolvable-cds-is-refused` decides a case where the REFERENCE fails to resolve a CDS; here the reference is fine and it is the DESCRIPTION that carries `?`. This record is about a description that explicitly declines to give a coordinate, whatever the reference holds.

clauses.quote: `?` (question mark) is used to indicate unknown positions (nucleotide or amino acid)
`?` (question mark) is used to indicate unknown positions (nucleotide or amino acid)

rulings.rationale:
The decision is to refuse — a house choice, with no governing clause. `CoordinateMapper::cds_to_tx` refuses a `c.?` position rather than coercing it into a concrete transcript coordinate. `c.?` states the position is unknown (`general.md:87`, restated `uncertain.md:12`); there is no coordinate for the conversion to answer with, and fabricating one is storable-but-wrong rather than a helpful default.

This replaces the mapper's previous behavior, which used to answer `c.?` with `c.1`'s own coordinate, because the unknown-position sentinel is integer `0` and fell into the 5'UTR arm with zero displacement — quietly substituting the CDS start for "unknown."

The principle is imported, not invented: a plausible-but-wrong answer a consumer can persist is worse than a clean decline — the same shape as refusing `c.pterdel`/`c.qterdel`/`c.1del` (which likewise collapsed a no-coordinate input onto an ordinary base) and refusing `insN[341]` for asserting bases the input never named. `c.?` is the same pattern one converter over.

This is a house choice, not a clause ruling: the recommendations describe descriptions, not what a coordinate mapper must do with one — `general.md:87` says what `?` means, not what to do with it. Refusing and propagating the `?` are both consistent with that meaning; no clause governs the choice, and this must never be cited as conformance.

In scope, the guard is keyed on the raw unknown-position sentinel value, not on a narrower "is this unknown" predicate — so it also catches the sibling telomere/centromere-marker shapes that share the same sentinel, on their own terms. An offset does not make the base known (`c.?+5` is still refused). Positions either side of the sentinel (`c.1`, `c.-1`, `c.*1`) still convert normally — the guard is exact-sentinel, not a widened 5'UTR refusal.

In representation terms there is no impact on the normalization path — this documents an adjudication for behavior already shipped, not a new code change.
rulings.summary: Converting a 'c.?' (unknown) position toward a transcript coordinate is refused rather than coerced into a concrete position — a project choice, since fabricating a coordinate for an explicitly unknown one yields a storable-but-wrong result.

rulings.question: The `c.` axis has three numbering zones — `c.-n` upstream of the ATG (5'UTR), plain `c.n` in the CDS, and `c.*n` downstream of the stop (3'UTR) — and a cis allele's members can sit in different ones. To sort members into merge order, detect overlap, and decide the separation `general.md:33` keys on, ferro needs to compare two positions that may be in different zones. `background/numbering.md` defines each zone (`:21`, `:29`, `:30`) and the flat transcript numbering (`:52`) but states no rule for comparing a position in one zone against a position in another, and never speaks about alleles or members at all. On what basis are two cross-zone `c.` positions ordered?

house_choice.considered_and_rejected:
THE ZONED `(Region, base)` SCALAR (the arithmetic this module was built on). Rejected: each position is tagged with its `Region` and a region-local integer — positive in the CDS and 3'UTR, negative in the 5'UTR — and the base counter RESETS to 1 at each zone. `c.72` and the adjacent `c.*1` are one nucleotide apart on the transcript yet far apart in scalar space, so a comparison keyed on `(Region, base)` is not monotone across the transcript: it orders positions by the `Region` enum's declaration index rather than by where the bases actually sit, and a span numbered on two zones has no single scalar at all. That non-monotonicity is a fact about the arithmetic, not about HGVS — `c.72_*1` is an ordinary real range (`c.15_*1del` deletes across a stop codon) — and keying member order, overlap and separation on it is what makes the same variant sort, overlap and separate differently depending only on which zone a member's spelling names.

CITING THE SPEC FOR THE ORDER. Rejected: `background/numbering.md` defines the three zones and, at `:52`, the flat `n.` numbering `from the first to the last nucleotide of the reference sequence`, but it states no rule for comparing a position in one zone against one in another. It contains zero occurrences of `allele` and zero of `member`, and `refseq.md`'s two `allele` hits (`:264-265`) are the population-genetics sense, not cis-allele membership. So there is no clause to hold governing: the recommendations are silent on cross-zone comparison, which is `normalization-rules.md` rule 5's silent limb, and an ordering rule would be an upstream feature request rather than a bug report.

PRESERVING THE INPUT'S SPELLING OR PREVIOUSLY-SHIPPED ORDER. Rejected: `canonical-form-choice-when-both-legal` already decides that a canonical form is derived from the resulting sequence, not from the input's spelling or the previously-shipped string. Ordering members by anything the input happened to write in would reintroduce exactly the input-dependence that record removes.

MAKING THE ORDER A COMPARISON THAT REFUSES ACROSS ZONES (`join_pos` returning `None` for a cross-zone pair). Rejected as a comparison rule, though it is retained where a single one-zone axis genuinely IS needed. A refusal is the right answer for a pass that must render one interval on one axis; it is the WRONG answer for a pass that only COMPARES members, where a refused comparison does not make the pass conservative — it makes the boundary-crossing member INVISIBLE as a sibling (`#1482`), which is how `c.[15_*1del;15_*1insCC]` came to normalize into an allele ferro's own parser rejects.

clauses.quote: numbering starts with `c.1` at the **`A`** of the `ATG` translation initiation (start) codon and ends with the last nucleotide of the translation termination (stop) codon
nucleotides upstream (5') of the `ATG`-translation initiation codon (start) are marked with a `-` (hyphen-minus) and numbered `c.-1`, `c.-2`, `c.-3`, etc., going further upstream
nucleotides downstream (3') of the translation termination codon (stop) are marked with a `*` (asterisk) and numbered `c.*1`, `c.*2`, `c.*3`, etc., going further downstream
nucleotide numbering is `n.1`, `n.2`, `n.3`, ..., etc., from the first to the last nucleotide of the reference sequence.

rulings.rationale:
This is a house choice (rule 5, silent limb), decided: two c. positions in different numbering zones (c.-n / c.n / c.*n) are ordered by their transcript-sequence offset — the flat coordinate numbering.md:52 counts n.1..n.length along — not by the c. spelling. Never cite the spec for this order: it defines the zones but is silent on comparing across them.

The map: each zone is one affine shift onto the transcript sequence — c.n (CDS) -> n + cds_start - 1; c.-n (5'UTR) -> cds_start - n; c.*n (3'UTR) -> cds_end + n — so c.-1 < c.1 < c.72 < c.*1 in true base order. A naive (Region, base) scalar instead orders by the Region enum's declaration index and wrongly puts c.72 before c.-1. The same map widens (region_span_delta) to the two n. regions outside the served sequence, for comparison only, so a member with no readable base is still ordered against its siblings rather than dropped.

This is a house choice rather than a clause ruling because numbering.md defines the zones (:21, :29, :30) and the flat n. numbering (:52) but states no cross-zone comparison rule, and no clause anywhere addresses comparing positions across zones.

In relation to other records: this is the ordering counterpart of c-and-n-positions-are-flat-transcript-offsets, which decides the coordinate space a single c./n. number lives in; this record decides how two such offsets in different zones compare. It is consistent with canonical-form-choice-when-both-legal — a transcript-coordinate order doesn't depend on how a member was spelled.

The scope: the comparison-side passes (cross-zone overlap/separation detection, dropping an identity member covered by a boundary-crossing sibling) already convert each endpoint onto the transcript offset before comparing; this record makes that policy explicit and pins it. It does not itself change the canonical-coalesced merge arm's own seam handling at the CDS/UTR boundaries — that is separate code work, disclosed by whatever change lands it, not by this record. join_pos's cross-zone refusal is retained where a pass genuinely can express only one single-zone axis: a refusal there means "this pass can't express that span," never "that span is malformed."

There is no representation impact from this record — it documents a policy the comparison passes already enforce.
rulings.summary: Two `c.` positions in different numbering zones (`c.-n`/`c.n`/`c.*n`) are ordered by their flat transcript-sequence offset, not by the `c.` spelling — a house choice under `normalization-rules.md` rule 5's silent limb, because the recommendations define the zones but state no rule for comparing across them.

rulings.question: A mosaic (`/`) or chimeric (`//`) substitution allele carries one member describing a variant nucleotide and one describing the reference (`=`). Ferro accepted a variant-first spelling (`c.85T>C/=`) and left it as authored, neither reordering it nor refusing it. `DNA/substitution.md:49` states the reference allele is "always described first", but the clause is non-normative prose. Does ferro reorder to reference-first, refuse the variant-first spelling, or leave it alone?
rulings.summary: A two-member mosaic (`/`) or chimeric (`//`) substitution allele is written reference-allele-first, so `c.85T>C/=` becomes `c.85=/T>C`, because the spec always describes the reference first; the variant-first spelling is reordered, not refused.

clauses.quote: irrespective of the frequency in which each nucleotide was found, the reference is always described first
irrespective of the frequency in which each nucleotide was found, the reference is always described first

rulings.rationale:
OPERATOR RULING, 2026-08-16 (#2034) — REORDER TO REFERENCE-FIRST. A two-member mosaic/chimeric SUBSTITUTION allele is emitted reference-allele-first: `c.85T>C/=` normalizes to `c.85=/T>C`, and the chimeric `//` analogue to `c.85=//T>C`. The variant-first spelling is not refused; it is rewritten.

AUTHORITY. `substitution.md:49` states it outright — "irrespective of the frequency in which each nucleotide was found, the reference is always described first" — and `:47` publishes the target `LRG_199t1:c.85=/T>C` as the spec's own worked mosaic example. The clause is lowercase prose, not an RFC 2119 keyword (per this repository's reading of the spec almost nothing in `recommendations/` is normative), so it is cited as GOVERNING in the sense of a positive statement of the rule ferro follows, not as a MUST. It aligns with the project's canonical-form doctrine (`canonical-form-choice-when-both-legal`): the form is derived rather than preserved from the input's spelling, and reference-first spellings are already fixed points, so this makes the two spellings of one mosaic converge on the one the spec prints.

WHY REORDER RATHER THAN REFUSE. Refusing the variant-first spelling in strict was the alternative the issue enumerated. It is rejected on the same ground `absolute-prohibition-enforcement-stage` gives for output conformance: accepting a non-conformant input and normalizing it to the conformant form trades nothing, and a mode-dependent refusal would leave lenient/silent still emitting the disfavoured order. Reordering fixes every mode at once.

SCOPE — SUBSTITUTION ONLY, DELIBERATELY. The ruling reaches a substitution beside a reference allele (`=`), which is the shape the issue names and the only one where reference-first is unambiguous: the reference-first compact form is `<pos>=/<edit>` and there is exactly one. A RANGE edit (`del`/`dup`) is OUT OF SCOPE and left as authored, because its reference-first spelling is ambiguous between the position-identity form `c.79_80=/del` and the whole-entity-identity form `c.=/79_80del`, and the spec does not adjudicate between them. A three-or-more-member mosaic, and a mosaic of two real edits (no reference member), are also out of scope — there is no single reference allele to move to the front. Those cases fall through unchanged and are owed their own ruling if raised.

MECHANISM. Implemented in `Normalizer::normalize_allele` via `reorder_mosaic_chimeric_reference_first`: a two-member, non-predicted Mosaic/Chimeric allele whose first member is a certain substitution and whose second member is a certain reference identity the rebuild can absorb losslessly — a whole-entity `=`, or a position-bound identity CO-LOCATED with the substitution (`c.85=` beside `c.85T>C`) — is rewritten to `[<sub-location>=, <sub>]`, then re-dispatched. A position-bound identity at a DIFFERENT location is a screened region (`c.85T>C/c.60_70=`) carrying its own fact; reordering would discard it, so it — and any allele with an uncertain member (`c.(85T>C)/=`) — is left exactly as authored (#2107). The rewrite is idempotent — its output is spelled reference-first and no longer matches the guard — so the re-dispatch runs at most once.

REPRESENTATION IMPACT: a real, one-directional migration. Every previously-accepted variant-first mosaic/chimeric substitution whose reference member is a whole-entity or co-located identity (`<pos><ref>><alt>/=` and the `//` form) re-spells to reference-first; a non-co-located screened region (`c.85T>C/c.60_70=`) or an uncertain member is unaffected. The synthetic shape-family corpus has no mosaic/chimeric family, so a count from it would be a STRUCTURAL zero; the move is disclosed in the PR's `Representation-Change:` trailer and pinned by `tests/it/issue_2034_mosaic_chimeric_reference_first.rs`.
